The near-critical random bond FK-percolation model

Emile Avérous ††thanks: Université de Genève. E-mail: emile.averous@unige.ch, remy.mahfouf@unige.ch    Rémy Mahfouf11footnotemark: 1
Abstract

We study FK-percolation where the edge parameters are chosen as independent random variables in the near-critical regime. We show that if these parameters satisfy a natural centering condition around the critical point, then the quenched model typically exhibits critical behaviour at scales much larger than the deterministic characteristic length. More precisely, in a box of size NN, if the homogeneous model with deterministic edge parameter pp looks critical in the regime |p−pc|≤W|p-p_{c}|\leq\textrm{W}, then the quenched model with random edge parameters 𝐩\mathbf{p} that typically satisfy |𝐩−pc|≤W1/3|\mathbf{p}-p_{c}|\leq\textrm{W}^{1/3} looks critical, assuming some conjectured inequality on critical exponents, and up to logarithmic corrections. We also treat the special case of Bernoulli percolation, where we show that if one first samples non-degenerate independent random edge parameters centered around 12\frac{1}{2}, and then a percolation configuration on these edges, the quenched model almost surely looks critical at large scales.

1 Introduction

1.1 General context

The two-dimensional Fortuin–Kasteleyn (FK) random cluster model, introduced in [33], provides a unifying framework for studying several central models in statistical mechanics, including Bernoulli percolation (q=1q=1), the Ising model (q=2q=2), and the Potts model for general q≥1q\geq 1. It was developed as a representation of the Potts model through random subgraphs of a fixed domain, weighted by a bond parameter p∈(0,1)p\in(0;1) and the number of connected components raised to a power governed by another parameter q>0q>0. In the planar case with nearest-neighbour interactions, the FK model is conjectured to exhibit conformal invariance in the scaling limit at its critical point when q≤4q\leq 4, in agreement with predictions from conformal field theory (CFT) [9, 8] and the Coulomb gas formalism. In the infinite-volume limit, the critical point on the square lattice, given by pc​(q)=q⋅(1+q)−1p_{c}(q)=\sqrt{q}\cdot(1+\sqrt{q})^{-1}, has been rigorously established for over a decade [7], confirming the longstanding conjecture that it coincides exactly with the self-dual point. On the square lattice, the only value of qq for which precise and complete statements of conformal invariance are known is the so-called FK-Ising model (corresponding to q=2q=2). In this case, Smirnov’s breakthrough result [51] proved the conformal invariance of FK interfaces by showing their convergence to SLE⁡(16/3)\mathrm{SLE}(16/3), using the so-called Ising fermionic observables. This approach shares many features with another seminal result by the same author, namely the proof of the Cardy formula for critical percolation on the triangular lattice [52]. Beyond crossing probabilities, it was later shown in this case that interfaces converge to SLE⁡(6)\mathrm{SLE}(6) [53], and that the entire loop ensemble converges to CLE⁡(6)\mathrm{CLE}(6) [13]. To date, it appears that generalisations of fermionic observables techniques are insufficient to directly address conformal invariance for all parameters 1≤q≤41\leq q\leq 4, where the scaling limits of FK interfaces are conjectured to be described by the nested CLE⁡(κ)\mathrm{CLE}(\kappa) loop ensemble, where κ∈[4,6]\kappa\in[4,6] is liked to qq via the relation

q=−2​cos⁡(4​πκ).\sqrt{q}=-2\cos\left(\frac{4\pi}{\kappa}\right).

An extensive body of research on the critical FK model over the past decade [26, 29, 21, 36, 27, 28] has yielded numerous important results, significantly advancing our understanding of the model. In this context, two landmark developments are the recent proof of rotational invariance in the full-plane setting [22], and the convergence of the associated six-vertex model to the Gaussian Free Field (GFF) [23], both of which represent major steps toward establishing conformal invariance.

It is widely believed that all reasonable statistical mechanics models exhibit a rather specific type of behaviour near their critical point, notably through the existence of the so-called critical exponents, which link the large-scale properties of the critical model to the behaviour of near-critical models. Among other things, the connectivity properties, cluster density, susceptibility, and the regularity of the free energy are expected to follow algebraic laws near the critical point. Moreover, these critical exponents are predicted to be related to one another through elegant relations originating from physics [31, 32], as recalled in [25, Introduction]. In [25], Duminil-Copin and Manolescu provided a rigorous proof that, assuming the existence of these exponents, they indeed satisfy the relations conjectured by physicists. Their results extend Kesten’s scaling relations [38] (see also [44]), originally proved for Bernoulli percolation (where independence of edges plays a crucial role), to the full range of parameters 1≤q≤41\leq q\leq 4. Understanding the precise behaviour of near-critical model exactly at its scaling window remains an active area of research for general FK models. Let us still mention that significantly more is known in the case of the near-critical FK-Ising model [6, 20, 47, 48, 46, 14, 56], where the extension of Ising fermionic observable techniques to the massive regime has led to substantial progress, in line with analogous results in the dimer context [15, 49, 11].

Once a refined understanding of critical models has been achieved, a natural question arises -that also connects to physical experiments- concerning the behaviour of critical models in random environments, particularly those that might average out to the deterministic critical setting. One may ask what happens if the bond parameters of the random cluster model are first randomly sampled, and one then performs statistical mechanics in this random environment. This is in the spirit of the famous (and still largely open) question concerning the critical behaviour of the random bond Ising model [16, 50, 43]. It is believed that for general FK models, such questions fall within the broader meta-principle of universality in statistical mechanics, which roughly states that the macroscopic behaviour at criticality should not be influenced by microscopic details, provided the parameters are tuned appropriately. In this setting, the critical parameter for the model in a random environment should almost surely (with respect to the randomness of the environment) exist and be well-defined, although it is generally different from the deterministic critical one. The study of statistical mechanics models in random environments remains largely unexplored, with the notable exception of random walks, for which homogenisation techniques yield rather precise results (see, e.g. [30, 37, 3]). For the random cluster model in a random environment, one notable result is the continuity of the quenched phase transition [1, 2].

In most of the present paper, we focus on the regime 1<q≤41<q\leq 4 and study weakly random environments, where the deviation from the homogeneous critical parameter in a box of size NN is modelled by independent random variables on each edge, centred at the critical point, with variances tending to zero as N→∞N\to\infty. Our main result is that, under mild assumptions, the weak randomness of the environment around the critical point averages out effectively, keeping the system in its critical phase. In particular, we show that, with high probability over the environment, one can allow random variables whose standard deviation from the critical point is cubicly larger than the intrinsic deterministic critical window of the model, while still remaining within the critical phase at all scales. In all of these cases, had one replaced the deviation from criticality by its absolute value (i.e., enforcing a fixed deterministic offset), the system would have been significantly off-critical. We apply an approach similar to the one in [42], moving continuously the random environment from the deterministic critical point to the desired random one.

We also give special attention to the case of Bernoulli percolation, where we prove that it is possible to take bond parameters whose standard deviation from the self-dual parameter is, in the exact Gaussian case, O(log(N)−1/2)O(\log(N)^{-1/2}) in a box of size NN, still ensuring criticality at every scale. Moreover, by leveraging noise sensitivity results [10, 34], we observe that it is even possible to allow macroscopic deviations (i.e., deviations don’t go to 00 as NN goes to ∞\infty), centred at the critical point, while retaining critical behaviour at large scales. For instance, we establish an asymptotic version of Cardy’s formula that holds with high probability over the environment. As an concrete example, one can sort for each vertex vv of the triangular lattice 𝒯\mathcal{T}, a random bond parameter 𝐩v∈{14,34}\mathbf{p}_{v}\in\{\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}\}, whose average is 𝐄⁡[pv]=12\mathbf{E}[p_{v}]=\frac{1}{2}, creating a random environment 𝔭=(𝐩v)v∈𝒯\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{T}} for some probability measure 𝐏\mathbf{P}. Consider the percolation ϕ𝔭\phi_{\mathfrak{p}} whose weights are given by 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. Then, with high 𝐏\mathbf{P}-probability, the percolation measure ϕ𝔭\phi_{\mathfrak{p}} satisfies the Cardy formula at large scale. This means that, the quenched percolation satisfies (with high 𝐏\mathbf{P}-probability), the Cardy formula at large scale, exactly as its annealed version ϕ𝐄⁡[𝔭]\phi_{\mathbf{E}[\mathfrak{p}]}, which corresponds to the critical deterministic Bernoulli percolation on the triangular lattice. In particular, it appears that the for Bernoulli percolation, the quenched disorder is irrelevant.

1.2 Setting and graph notations

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite subgraph of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} and define its boundary as ∂G:={v∈V⁡(G):v​ is incident to at least one edge outside of ​G}\partial G:=\{v\in V(G):v\text{ is incident to at least one edge outside of }G\}. We call a boundary condition ξ\xi a partition of the set ∂G\partial G. Among all possible boundary conditions, we highlight two special ones, the so called wired boundary conditions ξ=1\xi=1 corresponding to the partition {∂G}\{\partial G\} where all the vertices of ∂G\partial G are wired together as a single vertex, and the free boundary conditions ξ=0\xi=0 coresponding to the partition made of singletons, where no vertices of ∂G\partial G are wired together. We are now going to define a probability measure on random subgraphs of GG.

Definition 1.1 (Planar FK-percolation).

Given q≥1q\geq 1 and p∈(0,1)p\in(0;1), one can define the FK-percolation probability measure ϕG,p,qξ\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi} on configurations ω∈{0;1}E\omega\in\{0;1\}^{E} by setting

ϕG,p,qξ​[ω]:=1ZG,p,qξ​p|ω|​(1−p)|E\ω|​qk⁡(ωξ),\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}[\omega]:=\frac{1}{Z^{\xi}_{G,p,q}}p^{|\omega|}(1-p)^{|E\backslash\omega|}q^{k(\omega^{\xi})}, (1.1)

where |ω||\omega| denotes the number of vertices in the configuration ω\omega, k⁡(ωξ)k(\omega^{\xi}) the number of connected components of ω\omega when identifying boundary vertices in the same part of ξ\xi and ZG,p,qξZ^{\xi}_{G,p,q} is the partition function of the model, which is chosen so that ϕG,p,qξ​[⋅]\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}[\cdot] is a probability measure.

In the case where the bonds weights are not uniform and given by p¯=(pe)e∈E\underline{p}=(p_{e})_{e\in E}, one can generalise the previous definition setting

ϕG,p¯,qξ​[ω]:=1ZG,p¯,q​qk⁡(ωξ)​∏e∈ωpe​∏e∉ω(1−pe).\phi_{G,\underline{p},q}^{\xi}[\omega]:=\frac{1}{Z_{G,\underline{p},q}}q^{k(\omega^{\xi})}\prod\limits_{e\in\omega}p_{e}\prod\limits_{e\not\in\omega}(1-p_{e}). (1.2)

An edge ee is called open in ω\omega if ω⁡(e)=1\omega(e)=1, and closed otherwise. For two vertices v,v′∈G∪∂Gv,v^{\prime}\in G\cup\partial G, we define the event v​⟷𝜔​v′v\overset{\omega}{\longleftrightarrow}v^{\prime}, or simply v⟷v′v\longleftrightarrow v^{\prime} to be the event that the two vertices v,v′v,v^{\prime} belong to the same connected component in ω\omega. In the same way, for two (disjoint) subsets A,BA,B of GG, define A​⟷𝜔​BA\overset{\omega}{\longleftrightarrow}B or simply A⟷BA\longleftrightarrow B to be the event that there exist v∈A,v′∈Bv\in A,v^{\prime}\in B such that v⟷v′v\longleftrightarrow v^{\prime}. This model of dependent percolation is a generalisation of the usual independent bond percolation percolation on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} (corresponding to q=1q=1), interpolating also the so-called FK-Ising model (corresponding to q=2q=2). The dual of the lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} is (ℤ2)⋆:=ℤ2+(12;12)(\mathbb{Z}^{2})^{\star}:=\mathbb{Z}^{2}+(\frac{1}{2};\frac{1}{2}), corresponding to faces of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}. Each edge e∈Ee\in E can be mapped to the associated dual edge e⋆e^{\star} that links the two faces separated by ee. One can now define the dual configuration ω⋆\omega^{\star} as a graph on G⋆G^{\star} by setting

ω⋆​(e⋆):=1−ω⁡(e).\omega^{\star}(e^{\star}):=1-\omega(e). (1.3)

In the case where the random cluster on GG is chosen with boundary conditions ξ\xi equal to 00 or 11, the duality can even be extended as a probability measures on clusters ω⋆∈G⋆∪∂G⋆\omega^{\star}\in G^{\star}\cup\partial G^{\star}, with boundary conditions ξ⋆=1−ξ\xi^{\star}=1-\xi.

To circumvent some additional technicalities appearing when dealing with the uniqueness of the infinite volume measure, a fair share of our work is done on the torus, which requires changing slightly the above definition to take into account the non-planar nature of the torus. Let us state once and for all that all the results presented in the present paper can be easily transferred to the planar case.

For N≥1N\geq 1, set 𝕋N:=(ℤ/N​ℤ)2\mathbb{T}_{N}:=(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{2} the standard torus of width NN, whose edges are denoted by ENE_{N}. In that context, one can make a slightly different definition of the random cluster model. Note that the torus does not have a boundary, so there is no need to specify boundary conditions in the definition. In the following, a cluster is called non-contractible if it contains a path with non-trivial winding around the torus, and contractible otherwise.

Definition 1.2 (Torus FK-percolation).

Given q≥1q\geq 1 and p¯=(pe)e∈𝕋N\underline{p}=(p_{e})_{e\in\mathbb{T}_{N}} one can define the FK-percolation probability measure ϕ𝕋N,p,q\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p,q} on {0;1}EN\{0;1\}^{E_{N}} by setting

ϕ𝕋N,p¯,q​[ω]:=qs⁡(ω)Z𝕋N,p¯,q​qk⁡(ω)​∏e∈ωpe​∏e∉ω(1−pe),\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q}[\omega]:=\frac{\sqrt{q}^{s(\omega)}}{Z_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q}}q^{k(\omega)}\prod\limits_{e\in\omega}p_{e}\prod\limits_{e\not\in\omega}(1-p_{e}), (1.4)

where |ω||\omega|, k⁡(ω)k(\omega) are defined as above, Z𝕋N,p,qZ_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p,q} is the partition function of the model and

  • •

    s⁡(ω)=0s(\omega)=0 is all clusters of ω\omega are contractible

  • •

    s⁡(ω)=1s(\omega)=1 if there exists at least one non-contractible cluster in ω\omega and one non-contractible cluster in ω⋆\omega^{\star}.

  • •

    s⁡(ω)=2s(\omega)=2 if all clusters of ω⋆\omega^{\star} are contractible.

The modification in the definition compared to the planar case is encoded in the term qs⁡(ω)\sqrt{q}^{s(\omega)} which is added to make the model self-dual in the homogeneous bond case, using the fact that for any configuration ω\omega, one has s⁡(ω)=2−s⁡(ω∗)s(\omega)=2-s(\omega^{*}) (see [7] or [18, Exercise 28]). One could have in principle used a definition without the qs⁡(ω)\sqrt{q}^{s(\omega)} which would have led to the same large scale properties of the critical model, since this factor is always between 11 and qq.

In the last two decades, several groundbreaking results provided a very refined understanding of the sharp phase transition of the FK-random cluster models on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, with a specific focus on the large scale behaviour at critical model. The identification of the critical point was made by Beffara and Duminil-Copin in [7] using the self-duality of the model on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} and differential equations on the probability of crossing large topological rectangles. More precisely, the critical point pc​(q)p_{c}(q) is given by the self-dual parameter ps​d​(q)p_{sd}(q) that makes the model self-dual (i.e. ω​=(d)​ω⋆\omega\overset{(d)}{=}\omega^{\star}), which is given explicitly by

ps​d​(q)=pc​(q):=q1+q.p_{sd}(q)=p_{c}(q):=\frac{\sqrt{q}}{1+\sqrt{q}}. (1.5)

In the range of parameters 1≤q≤41\leq q\leq 4, some sharp dichotomy in the connectivity properties of the full-plane model appears. The restriction of this is two-fold. In a nutshell, if p<pc​(q)p<p_{c}(q) the model is called sub-critical and the probability that two vertices are connected decays to 00 exponentially fast in the distance separating them. Conversely if p>pc​(q)p>p_{c}(q), the model is called super-critical and the connection probability between vertices converges, exponentially in the distance separating the vertices, to some positive constant. The most interesting and delicate question to treat is that of the behaviour of the model at its critical point pc​(q)p_{c}(q). In that case, the probability that two points are connected decays polynomially fast in their distance and the model displays some intermediate behaviour. Let us also mention (see [19]) that when q>4q>4, the phase transition of the model is discontinuous and correlations at criticality for the full plane free measure decay exponentially fast. On the other hand, when q<1q<1, the models is negatively associated, meaning that increasing events disfavour each other.

The scaling limit of the model is conjectured to be conformally invariant, which was only proven by Smirnov in the special case of site percolation on the triangular lattice [52] and the Ising model [51]. Let us highlight the recent result that all FK-percolation models with 1≤q≤41\leq q\leq 4 are rotationally invariant at large scales [22], providing some landmark progress towards the rigorous identification of the full-plane scaling limit, which is strengthened by the recent identification of the scaling limit of the associated 66 vertex model [23] in the full-plane.

To date, one of the best understood features of the critical self-dual models is some coexistence phenomenon of large macroscopic primal and dual clusters that surround each other. One way to quantify this phenomenology is the so-called Russo-Seymour-Welsh (RSW) [39] strong box crossing property which reads as follows. Let ΛN:=[−N;N]2\Lambda_{N}:=[-N;N]^{2} the box centred at the origin and define 𝒞⁡(ΛN)\mathscr{C}(\Lambda_{N}) to be the event that there exists an open circuit linking the left to the right vertical boundaries of ΛN\Lambda_{N}. Then there exists an absolute constant c⁡(q)>0c(q)>0 (which, crucially, does not depend on NN) [7, 28] such that

c⁡(q)≤ϕΛ2​N,pc​(q),q0​[ there exist a vertical crossing in ​ΛN]≤1−c⁡(q),c(q)\leq\phi_{\Lambda_{2N},p_{c}(q),q}^{0}\Big[\textrm{ there exist a vertical crossing in }\Lambda_{N}\Big]\leq 1-c(q), (1.6)

where FK-measure is chosen with the free boundary conditions. One can fix some universal δ>0\delta>0 small enough (depending on qq), whose exact value is not relevant for the theory and can be explicitly recovered by [25, Theorem 2.1]. Defining the event 𝒞⁡(ΛN)\mathscr{C}(\Lambda_{N}) to be the existence of a vertical crossing between the boundaries of ΛN\Lambda_{N}, then for the unique full-plane Gibbs measure ϕp\phi_{p} on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, one can define the characteristic length by setting

L​(p)=L​(p,q):=inf{R≥1,ϕp​[𝒞⁡(ΛN)]∉[δ;1−δ]}∈[1;∞].\textrm{L}(p)=\textrm{L}(p,q):=\inf\Big\{R\geq 1,\phi_{p}[\mathscr{C}(\Lambda_{N})]\not\in[\delta;1-\delta]\Big\}\in[1;\infty]. (1.7)

The duality and the sharpness of the phase transition in [7] ensure that L​(p)<∞\textrm{L}(p)<\infty when p≠pc​(q)p\neq p_{c}(q) while L​(pc​(q))=∞\textrm{L}(p_{c}(q))=\infty by (1.6). Informally speaking, the characteristic length is the maximal size of a box for which the FK-model of parameters (p,q)(p,q) still behaves like the critical one (pc​(q),q)(p_{c}(q),q), at least in terms of crossing events. One can define similarly the critical window on the box ΛN\Lambda_{N} by setting

W(N)=W(N,q):=infp∈[0,1]{|p−pc(q)|,∃ a square S⊂ΛN,ϕp[𝒞(S)]∉[δ;1−δ]}.\textrm{W}(N)=\textrm{W}(N,q):=\inf\limits_{p\in[0,1]}\Big\{|p-p_{c}(q)|,\,\exists\textrm{ a square }S\subset\Lambda_{N},\,\phi_{p}[\mathscr{C}(S)]\not\in[\delta;1-\delta]\Big\}. (1.8)

The critical window and characteristic length can be interpreted as being two parametrisations of the set of pairs (R,p)(R,p) such that, under ϕp\phi_{p}, one has some RSW property at scale RR. From this, one gets that these functions are essentially inverses of each other, and it can be shown that they satisfy the identities L​(pc​(q)±W​(N))≍N\textrm{L}(p_{c}(q)\pm\textrm{W}(N))\asymp N and W​(L​(p))≍|p−pc​(q)|\textrm{W}(\textrm{L}(p))\asymp|p-p_{c}(q)|. In the case of Bernoulli bond percolation, one of the scaling relations proved by Kesten [38] relates the critical window W​(N)\textrm{W}(N) to some geometric quantity called the 44-arm event probability at criticality π4,pc​(N)\pi_{4,p_{c}}(N), through the identity W​(N)≍N−2​π4,pc​(N)−1\textrm{W}(N)\asymp N^{-2}\pi_{4,p_{c}}(N)^{-1}. For general FK models (with 1<q≤41<q\leq 4), one can define the so-called mixing rates Δpc​(N)\Delta_{p_{c}}(N)

Δpc(N):=ϕpc​(q),q1[0⟷∂ΛN]−ϕpc​(q),q0[0⟷∂ΛN].\Delta_{p_{c}}(N):=\phi^{1}_{p_{c}(q),q}[0\longleftrightarrow\partial\Lambda_{N}]-\phi^{0}_{p_{c}(q),q}[0\longleftrightarrow\partial\Lambda_{N}]. (1.9)

Informally speaking, the mixing rate measures precisely the influence of boundary conditions for connection probabilities for the model at criticality. One of the core innovations of [25] is that for q∈(1,4]q\in(1,4], one can replace the stability of the 44-arm event probabilities below the characteristic length by the stability of the mixing rates to derive the scaling relations. Note that when q=1q=1, the bond independence of the edges enforces that Δpc​(N)=0\Delta_{p_{c}}(N)=0 for any N≥1N\geq 1, making this quantity useless. One of the main results of [25] is the identity

W​(N)≍N−2​Δpc​(N)−1,\textrm{W}(N)\asymp N^{-2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(N)^{-1}, (1.10)

which allows to rewrite the scaling window (inherently tied to the off-critical behaviour of the model) to the stochastic geometry at criticality.

Notational convention In the entire paper, for f,gf,g two functions that may depend on the bond parameter pp, we denote respectively f≍gf\asymp g, f≲gf\lesssim g and f≳gf\gtrsim g the fact that there exist some universal contants CC only depending on 1≤q≤41\leq q\leq 4, and the constants appearing in Definition 1.3, such that one has C−1​f≤g≤C​fC^{-1}f\leq g\leq Cf (respectively C−1​f≤gC^{-1}f\leq g, g≤C​fg\leq Cf). When f≲gf\lesssim g, we also use sometimes the standard notation f=O⁡(g)f=O(g). Moreover, all the constants will implicitly be allowed to depend on the δ\delta parameter of the RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) strong box crossing property of Definition 1.4.

1.3 Main results

The main goal of the present paper is to define a similar notion of critical window in the case of a random environment, meaning here that one first sorts the edge weights of the random cluster model under some probability measure 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} and then studies the random cluster model attached to these weights. We will stick here to the case where the random weights are centred around the self-dual value in the deterministic case, with an addition natural condition on its variance detailed below. In a nutshell, the main output of the present paper is that randomness when sorting the environment under 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} averages very well and preserves the critical phase of the model way beyond the deterministic parameters, at least with a very high 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}-probability. Let us fix some parameter 1<q≤41<q\leq 4, excluding the case of percolation which will be treated separately, and add a few notations. First define, for each qq, the value

μ⁡(q):=q−12​q.\mu(q):=\frac{q-1}{2\sqrt{q}}. (1.11)
Definition 1.3 (Properties (⋆)NA(\star)_{N}^{\text{A}} and (⋆)NB(\star)_{N}^{\text{B}}).

Consider a collection of random variables 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈EN\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} indexed by the edges of 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}, which will be called a random environment. For each e∈ENe\in E_{N}, denote by σe:=𝔼​[(𝐩e−pc​(q))2]12{\sigma_{e}:=\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q))^{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}}} the standard deviation of 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e}. Consider the following properties for the random environment 𝔭\mathfrak{p}:

  1. 1.

    (Independence) The variables (𝐩e)∈EN(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{\in E_{N}} are mutually independent.

  2. 2.
    1. A)

      (Naive centering) Their first moment is centred at pc​(q)p_{c}(q) i.e.

      𝔼𝐏N​[𝐩e]=pc​(q).\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{P}_{N}}[\mathbf{p}_{e}]=p_{c}(q).
    2. B)

      (Natural centering) Their first and second moments are related by

      𝔼𝐏N​[𝐩e]=pc​(q)−μ⁡(q)​σe2+O⁡(σe3).\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{P}_{N}}[\mathbf{p}_{e}]=p_{c}(q)-\mu(q)\sigma_{e}^{2}+O(\sigma_{e}^{3}).

      where μ⁡(q)\mu(q) is defined above and the constant in OO is uniform in NN.

  3. 3.

    (Exponential tails) For each e∈ENe\in E_{N}, the tails of 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} satisfy

    ∀s>0,ℙN[|𝐩e−pc(q)|>s]≲exp(−c⋅(sσe))\forall s>0,\quad\mathbb{P}_{N}\Big[|\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q)|>s\Big]\lesssim\exp\left(-c\cdot\left(\frac{s}{\sigma_{e}}\right)\right)

    for some fixed c>0c>0 independent of NN.

We say that the variables 𝔭=(𝐩e)e\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e} satisfy (⋆)NA(\star)_{N}^{\text{A}} (respectively (⋆)NB(\star)_{N}^{\text{B}}) if they satisfy properties 1,2​A1,2\text{A} and 33 (respectively 1,2​B1,2\text{B} and 33). Note that these definitions implicitly depend on the constants O,≲O,\lesssim and the constant cc, which we do not mention for the sake of readability. In particular, all the constants appearing in the following theorems might depend on O,≲,cO,\lesssim,c.

The first condition is set to run some central limit theorem regarding the random environment 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}, while the second condition on moments comes from some natural approximate self-duality for the first two moments of the random variables 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e}, as we want both crossing probabilities of the primal and dual models not to degenerate. The third condition is only technical and can be relaxed. In principle, all the results in the present paper also hold if the 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} have stretched exponential tails, with modified estimates. We also do not assume that the variables 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} are [0,1][0,1]-valued, but their tails ensure that, with high probability, all of the 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} belong to [0,1][0,1] as long as the σe\sigma_{e} go to 00 fast enough in NN (see e.g. the discussion at the beginning of Section 3.1). Except for the special case of Bernoulli percolation, the spirit of the present paper is to send Σ𝔭:=maxe∈EN⁡σe→0\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}:=\max_{e\in E_{N}}\sigma_{e}\to 0 as the size of 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} goes to ∞\infty, but at a speed which is much slower than the deterministic critical window W​(N)\textrm{W}(N). In particular, randomness on the environment produces with a high 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} probability some FK model which is a mixture of locally subcritical and supercritical models which average to a critical model on a much larger scale than the deterministic one. To make the setup more concrete, let us present two families of i.i.d. random variables that satisfy respectively (⋆)NA(\star)_{N}^{\text{A}} and (⋆)NB(\star)_{N}^{\text{B}} :

  1. 1.

    Given a family (X(e))e∈EN(X^{(e)})_{e\in E_{N}} of i.i.d. centred ±1\pm 1 random variables and some non-negative σN\sigma_{N}, set

    (A)\displaystyle(\textrm{A})\quad 𝐩e=pc​(q)+σN⋅X(e)=pc​(q)±σN\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{e}=p_{c}(q)+\sigma_{N}\cdot X^{(e)}=p_{c}(q)\pm\sigma_{N}
    (B)\displaystyle(\textrm{B})\quad 𝐩e=pc​(q)+σN⋅X(e)−μ⁡(q)⋅σN2=pc​(q)±σN−μ⁡(q)⋅σN2.\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{e}=p_{c}(q)+\sigma_{N}\cdot X^{(e)}-\mu(q)\cdot\sigma_{N}^{2}=p_{c}(q)\pm\sigma_{N}-\mu(q)\cdot\sigma_{N}^{2}.
  2. 2.

    Given a family (𝒩(e))e∈EN(\mathcal{N}^{(e)})_{e\in E_{N}} of i.i.d. standard centred gaussian variables and some non-negative σN\sigma_{N}, set

    (A)\displaystyle(\textrm{A})\quad 𝐩e=pc​(q)+σN⋅𝒩(e),\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{e}=p_{c}(q)+\sigma_{N}\cdot\mathcal{N}^{(e)},
    (B)\displaystyle(\textrm{B})\quad 𝐩e=pc​(q)+σN⋅𝒩(e)−μ⁡(q)⋅σN2.\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{e}=p_{c}(q)+\sigma_{N}\cdot\mathcal{N}^{(e)}-\mu(q)\cdot\sigma_{N}^{2}.

When σN→0\sigma_{N}\to 0 as N→∞N\to\infty, both families of variables satisfy respectively (⋆)NA(\star)_{N}^{\text{A}} and (⋆)NB(\star)_{N}^{\text{B}}, while the σN\sigma_{N} scaling ensures that Σ𝔭→0\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\to 0. The Gaussian setup of the second item is of crucial interest and will be treated separately, as it allows to deduce the general case via some form of Skorokhod embedding theorem.

In the random non-homogeneous setup, the FK percolation measure with bonds inherited from 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} lacks translation invariance and self-duality. Therefore, to state some criticality conditions, one needs to check that crossing events (both primal and dual) are preserved in all of a given torus. This is the classical Russo-Seymour-Welsh (RSW) theory, which leads us to the following definition.

Definition 1.4.

Let δ>0\delta>0 be some small enough positive constant. A 22 by 11 rectangle in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} is a rectangle ℛ\mathcal{R} of dimensions R×R/2R\times R/2 or R/2×RR/2\times R in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}, with 1≤R≤N/41\leq R\leq N/4. For such an ℛ\mathcal{R}, let ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} be the twice bigger rectangle with the same center as ℛ\mathcal{R}. Denote 𝒞h​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}_{h}(\mathcal{R}) (respectively 𝒞h⋆​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}^{\star}_{h}(\mathcal{R})) the event that ℛ\mathcal{R} is crossed in the horizontal direction by a primal (respectively dual) path, and 𝒞v​(ℛ),𝒞v⋆​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}_{v}(\mathcal{R}),\mathscr{C}^{\star}_{v}(\mathcal{R}) the same events but for a vertical crossing. For an environment p¯=(pe)e∈EN\underline{p}=(p_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}, we say that the measure ϕ𝕋N,p¯,q\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q} satisfies the strong RSW property on the torus 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} for the parameter δ\delta if for any 22 by 11 rectangle ℛ⊂𝕋N\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N} one has

{ϕℛ′,p¯,q0​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)]≥δ,ϕℛ′,p¯,q1​[𝒞∙⋆​(ℛ)]≥δ,\begin{cases}\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\underline{p},q}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\geq\delta,\\ \phi^{1}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\underline{p},q}[\mathscr{C}^{\star}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\geq\delta,\end{cases}

for ∙=h\bullet=h and ∙=v\bullet=v. We denote RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) the set of measures ϕ𝕋N,p¯,q\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q} for which the strong RSW property with parameter δ\delta is satisfied on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}.

In our setup, individual edge weights could in principle get close to 00 or 11. Therefore, we take the convention that a rectangle of dimensions 2×12\times 1 or 1×21\times 2 is a single edge, so that the RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) property implies that each edge is open with some probability between δ\delta and 1−δ1-\delta, and this implies that for each edge e∈𝕋Ne\in\mathbb{T}_{N}, one has pe∈[δ,q⁡(1−δ)​(δ+q⁡(1−δ))−1]{p_{e}\in\big[\delta,q(1-\delta)\big(\delta+q(1-\delta)\big)^{-1}\big]}, remaining away from 00 and 11. It is standard to see (e.g. [25, Theorem 2.1] that the rectangle crossing introduced in Definition 1.4 implies a stronger version of the strong box crossing property, for both the primal and dual models. For example, assuming that ϕ𝕋N,p¯,q\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p},q} satisfies RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N), if we consider the FK measure on an annulus A⁡(R,2​R)=Λ2​R\ΛR⊂𝕋N{A(R,2R)=\Lambda_{2R}\backslash\Lambda_{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}} with free boundary conditions, then with probability bounded from below by a positive constant depending only on δ\delta, there is a primal cluster in A⁡(R,2​R)A(R,2R) surrounding the inner boundary of the annulus. A similar result holds for the dual model. We are now in position to state the first result of the paper, which proves that, when naively centerings the random bond parameters at the critical value, randomness with respect to the environment allows to deviate all coupling constants from the critical one inside 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} by some random variables whose standard deviation is of order W​(N)12\textrm{W}(N)^{\frac{1}{2}}.

Theorem 1.5.

Fix 1<q≤41<q\leq 4. Then there exists δ=δ⁡(q)>0\delta=\delta(q)>0 and c=c⁡(q)>0c=c(q)>0 such that the following holds. Let N≥1N\geq 1 be an integer and consider a random environment 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈𝕋N\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in\mathbb{T}_{N}} satisfying (⋆)NA(\star)_{N}^{\text{A}}. Define Σ𝔭:=maxe∈EN⁡σe\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}:=\max_{e\in E_{N}}\sigma_{e}. Then, assuming that Σ𝔭≤c⋅W​(N)1/2{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}, one has

𝐏N[ϕ𝕋N,𝔭,q∈RSW(δ,N)]>1−O(exp[−cNc⋅(W​(N)1/2Σ𝔭)1/2]).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p},q}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Big]>1-O\left(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\cdot\Bigg(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\Bigg)^{1/2}\Bigg]\right).

The previous statement shows that randomness in the environment sampled according to 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}, enhances the mixing between slightly subcritical and slightly supercritical bond parameters (chosen at random), whose standard deviation matches the square root of the original critical window, while preserving the model within its critical phase. This result can, in fact, be improved. Under the assumption (⋆)NA(\star)_{N}^{\text{A}}, the environmental randomness is, to first order, adapted to a linear deviation around the critical point. However, there is no a priori reason for the environment to linearise perfectly around criticality (except in the case of percolation). In particular, one can extend the expansion of a self-dual setup beyond the first moment by incorporating second-order terms. This correction leads to the refined condition (⋆)NB(\star)_{N}^{\text{B}}. Under this improved condition, one can in principle replace the critical window W​(N)\textrm{W}(N) by its cube root W​(N)1/3\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}, up to some sub-polynomial correction. More precisely, define

W~(N):=W(N)(∑r≤NrΔpc(r)4)−1/2.\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N):=\textrm{W}(N)\Big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\Big)^{-1/2}. (1.12)

Predictions from conformal field theory and the convergence to CLE [41, 25] suggest that Δpc​(r)≍r−ι⁡(q)\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)\asymp r^{-\iota(q)}, where ι⁡(q)≥12\iota(q)\geq\frac{1}{2}, with equality if and only if q=4q=4. In particular, one should have (∑r≤NrΔpc(r)4)−1/2≍1(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4})^{-1/2}\asymp 1 when 1<q<41<q<4, and (∑r≤NrΔpc(r)4)−1/2=N−o⁡(1){(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4})^{-1/2}=N^{-o(1)}} in the case q=4q=4. Let us mention an ongoing work [5], where notably the bound ι⁡(q)>14\iota(q)>\frac{1}{4} can be derived for all 1<q≤41<q\leq 4, while no other results are known except for the FK-Ising model. Therefore, assuming conformal invariance of the critical limiting model, one gets W~​(N)≍W​(N)\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)\asymp\textrm{W}(N), with a potential sub-polynomial correction when q=4q=4. One can now extend the critical window in a random environment to the cubic root of the original one, when working with a random environment naturally centred at pc​(q)p_{c}(q). Let us point out that in the following theorem, the estimates and the exponents in the logarithmic factors depend on the tail bounds for the 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e}, and better tail bounds would allow us to get better estimates. Recall that Σ𝔭\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}} is defined as Σ𝔭:=maxe∈EN⁡σe\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}:=\max_{e\in E_{N}}\sigma_{e}.

Theorem 1.6.

Fix 1<q≤41<q\leq 4. Then there exists δ=δ⁡(q)>0\delta=\delta(q)>0 and c=c⁡(q)>0c=c(q)>0 such that the following holds. For any N≥1N\geq 1, any random environment 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈EN\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} satisfying (⋆)NB(\star)_{N}^{\text{B}} and such that Σ𝔭≤c⋅W~​(N)1/3​log⁡(N)−2\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq c\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-2}, one has

𝐏N[ϕ𝕋N,𝔭,q∈RSW(δ,N)]>1−O(exp[−c⋅(W~​(N)1/3Σ𝔭)1/2]).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p},q}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Big]>1-O\left(\exp\left[-c\cdot\left(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\right]\right).

One should read the previous theorem keeping in mind the conjectured convergence of FK-percolation models towards CLE loop ensembles. In that setup, (see e.g. [25, Table Introduction]) there should exist ν=ν⁡(q)>0\nu=\nu(q)>0 such that W​(N)=N−ν+o⁡(1)\textrm{W}(N)=N^{-\nu+o(1)}. In the random environment, it is in principle possible to work with bond parameters whose standard deviation from the critical point satisfies maxe∈𝕋N⁡σe≍N−ν3+o⁡(1)≫N−ν\max_{e\in\mathbb{T}_{N}}\sigma_{e}\asymp N^{-\frac{\nu}{3}+o(1)}\gg N^{-\nu} while remaining in the critical phase of the model, at least with high 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}-probability. If one replaces 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈EN\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} by (pc​(q)+|𝐩e−pc​(q)|)e∈EN(p_{c}(q)+|\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q)|)_{e\in E_{N}}, the model would have exhibited a fairly off-critical behaviour. One could wonder about the existence of some (⋆)NC(\star)^{\text{C}}_{N} set of conditions on the random bonds 𝔭\mathfrak{p} that would have kept Σ𝔭\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}} allowing some even (polynomially) larger window than W​(N)1/3\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}. While we do not claim that finding such an environment 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is impossible, we argue in Section 4.3 that for an environment with independent bonds 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e}, the window W​(N)1/3\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3} is a natural barrier when only requiring approximate self-duality for the bond parameters. Still, one can explore some slightly less restrictive setup, allowing the bonds to be dependent. For instance, one can construct a model where the bond parameters are the sum of an i.i.d process at each edge, together with a correction (of much smaller order of magnitude) which takes into account all the edges in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}. Furthermore, the bond parameters in this interacting model should become essentially independent for edges far away from each other in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}. In this case, the (random) correction term is chosen in such a way that all the terms of the form ϕ𝕋N,𝔭,q​[𝒞​(ℛ)]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p},q}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})] have expectation their value at criticality ϕ𝕋N,pc,q​[𝒞​(ℛ)]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p_{c},q}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})]. We explain how to achieve this in the proof of the following result. To lighten notations, set Ξ⁡(N):=(∑r≤Nr​Δpc​(r)2)−1\Xi(N):=\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}\right)^{-1}.

Theorem 1.7.

Fix 1<q≤41<q\leq 4 and let 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈E\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E} a random environment satisfying (⋆)NB(\star)^{\text{B}}_{N}. There exist some positive constants δ,O,c1,2\delta,O,c_{1,2} such that if Σ𝔭≤c1⋅Ξ​(N)1/2​log⁡(N)−2\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq c_{1}\cdot\Xi(N)^{1/2}\log(N)^{-2}, one can construct some modified environment 𝔭~=(𝐩~e)e∈EN\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}=(\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} such that

  • •

    Under 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}, for each e∈ENe\in E_{N}, the difference |𝐩~e−𝐩e||\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}-\mathbf{p}_{e}| is of order Ξ(N)−1/2σe3\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\sigma_{e}^{3}, in the sense that

    ∀α>0,𝐏N[|𝐩~e−𝐩e|>α⋅Ξ(N)−1/2σe3]≲exp(−cα1/3).\forall\alpha>0,\quad\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[|\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}-\mathbf{p}_{e}|>\alpha\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\sigma_{e}^{3}\Big]\lesssim\exp(-c\alpha^{1/3}).
  • •

    One has

    𝐏N[ϕ𝕋N,𝔭~,q∈RSW(δ,N)]>1−O(exp[−c2⋅(Ξ​(N)1/2Σ𝔭)1/2]).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}},q}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Big]>1-O\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-c_{2}\cdot\left(\frac{\Xi(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\Bigg]\Bigg).

In words, the random correction to 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is typically of order Σ𝔭3≪Σ𝔭\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{3}\ll\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}. This slightly interacting model becomes of particular interest when 1<q≤21<q\leq 2 where Ξ⁡(N)\Xi(N) is expected to be constant (or logarithmic when q=2q=2), providing an already logarithmic near-critical window in the random environment, similarly to the result we derive below for percolation.

Let us now turn to the specific case of Bernoulli bond percolation, corresponding to the random cluster model with parameter q=1q=1. In this setting, we prove that the critical phase of the model in the random environment is preserved at every scale for random bond parameters centred at the critical point, even when allowing variable whose standard deviation is logarithmic in the size of the box. Moreover, if one only focuses on on the large scale crossing probabilities, we show, using a short noise sensitivity argument, that the critical phase of the model is preserved even with macroscopic deformation from the critical point, not requiring the variances to decay to 00 as N→∞N\to\infty. Before presenting precise results, let us define the natural moment condition on the random variables 𝔭\mathfrak{p} in the case q=1q=1, where the dependencies are linear with respect to each edge bond. This leads to the definition of the condition (⋆)Nq=1(\star)_{N}^{q=1}, given by

  1. 1.

    (Independence) The variables (𝐩e)∈EN(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{\in E_{N}} are mutually independent.

  2. 2.

    (Exact self-dual mean) They all have mean 𝔼𝐏N​[𝐩e]=pc​(1)=12\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{P}_{N}}[\mathbf{p}_{e}]=p_{c}(1)=\frac{1}{2}.

  3. 3.

    (Exponential tails) For each e∈ENe\in E_{N}, the tails of 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} satisfy

    ∀s>0,ℙN[|𝐩e−12|>s]≲exp(−c⋅(sσe))\forall s>0,\quad\mathbb{P}_{N}\Big[\big|\mathbf{p}_{e}-\frac{1}{2}\big|>s\Big]\lesssim\exp\left(-c\cdot\left(\frac{s}{\sigma_{e}}\right)\right)

    for some fixed c>0c>0 independent from NN.

We still denote σe:=𝔼​[(pe−12)2]1/2\sigma_{e}:=\mathbb{E}[(p_{e}-\tfrac{1}{2})^{2}]^{1/2} and Σ𝔭:=maxe∈𝕋N⁡σe\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}:=\max_{e\in\mathbb{T}_{N}}\sigma_{e}. In contrast to the general FK-percolation case with 1<q≤41<q\leq 4, one requires that the expectation of each pep_{e} be exactly 12\tfrac{1}{2}, and not merely close to it. Indeed, the self-duality condition for the random environment can be expressed via its first moment only. Also note that when defining RSW⁡(δ,N)\mathrm{RSW}(\delta,N) the boundary conditions (00 or 11) on the rectangle ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} used in Definition 1.4 are irrelevant. This allows us to state the following theorem, which establishes that the permissible deviations from criticality can be of order O⁡(log⁡(N)−O⁡(1))O(\log(N)^{-O(1)}) in the torus 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} while remaining in the critical phase at every scale.

Theorem 1.8.

There exists δ=δ⁡(q)>0\delta=\delta(q)>0 and c=c⁡(q)c=c(q), such that for any N≥1N\geq 1 and any random environment 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈EN\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} satisfying (⋆)Nq=1(\star)_{N}^{q=1} with Σ𝔭≤c⋅log⁡(N)−2\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}\leq c\cdot\log(N)^{-2}, one has

𝐏N[ϕ𝕋N,𝔭,1∈RSW(δ,N)]>1−O(exp[−c⋅(Σ𝔭)−1/2]).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p},1}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Bigg]>1-O\Bigg(\exp\Big[-c\cdot(\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}})^{-1/2}\Big]\Bigg). (1.13)

As one can see within the proof of this theorem, there are a priori no conceptual reason to only use our technique to near-critical random environments. In the simplified Gaussian case, one can continuously move the random environments from the critical one to the Gaussian one using i.i.d. Brownian motions. Along the deformation, the crossing probability in a rectangle, whose initial value is bounded away from 00 and 11, is a local martingale with some uniformly bounded (in the size of the rectangle and also in NN) quadratic variation, leaving some hope that one can control it up to some small but fixed positive time. Still, to carry out the main steps of our reasoning, it is essential to preserve criticality at every scale, meaning that we have to control crossing probabilities for all the O⁡(N3)O(N^{3}) 22 by 11 rectangles of 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}. Restricting to random variables with standard deviation O⁡(log⁡(N)−O⁡(1))O(\log(N)^{-O(1)}) is sufficient to control crossing probabilities in all the rectangles of 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}, via some crude large deviation principle. To go beyond this regime, one would like to develop some renormalisation argument, informally stating that if only a small fraction of the rectangles inside 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} become off-critical, then large-scale critical behaviour might persist. A more careful analysis shows that, using the same Brownian deformation process, the quadratic variation of the local martingales encoding crossing probabilities decays to 00 with the size of the box (improving the uniform positive bound mentioned few lines ago). This hints that one can try to shortcut such renormalisation argument using noise sensitivity of Bernoulli percolation [10], which turns out to be sufficient.

Let us precise the previous discussion for site percolation on the triangular lattice, whose conformal invariance has been proved in [52] (see also [53] for the rigorous derivation of the critical exponents). Consider the infinite lattice 𝒯\mathcal{T} made of equilateral triangles of edge length 11, where the segment [0,1]⊂ℂ[0,1]\subset\mathbb{C} is the side of one the triangles. Define the triangle 𝒯N\mathcal{T}_{N} whose three extremal vertices are located at AN=(−N2,0)A_{N}=(-\frac{N}{2};0), BN=(N2,0)B_{N}=(\frac{N}{2};0) and CN=(0,32​N)C_{N}=(0;\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}N). The (homogeneous) critical site percolation on the triangular lattice is a random colouring of the vertices of 𝒯N\mathcal{T}_{N}, where each site is coloured in blue or yellow with probability 12\frac{1}{2} and independently from the others. Fix some positive number x∈[0;1]x\in[0;1] and consider the point xN=(⌊(12−x)​N⌋,0)x_{N}=(\lfloor(\frac{1}{2}-x)N\rfloor,0). In this context, denote ϕ𝒯,12,1\phi_{\mathcal{T},\frac{1}{2},1} the fair site percolation measure on the infinite lattice 𝒯\mathcal{T}. One can define the crossing event

𝒞⁡([CN;AN],[xN;BN]):={[CN;AN]​ is connected to ​[xN;BN]​ by a blue path in ​𝒯N}.\mathscr{C}([C_{N};A_{N}],[x_{N};B_{N}]):=\Big\{[C_{N};A_{N}]\textrm{ is connected to }[x_{N};B_{N}]\textrm{ by a blue path in }\mathcal{T}_{N}\Big\}. (1.14)

The following beautiful theorem is due to Smirnov [52] settling Cardy’s conjecture for crossing probabilities of percolation. One simplified version reads as

Theorem 1.9 (Cardy-Smirnov formula [52]).

In the previous context

limN→∞ϕ𝒯,12,1​[𝒞⁡([CN;AN],[xN;BN])]=x.\lim\limits_{N\to\infty}\phi_{\mathcal{T},\frac{1}{2},1}\Bigg[\mathscr{C}([C_{N};A_{N}],[x_{N};B_{N}])\Bigg]=x. (1.15)

In our framework, we take advantage of the stability of crossing events to see that the Cardy formula is preserved when working with in a random environments, even with macroscopic deviation. Fix 0<ε≤120<\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{2} small enough. Similarly to the notations used for the square lattice, set 𝔭=(𝐩v)v∈𝒯\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{v})_{v\in\mathcal{T}} a random environment on the sites of 𝒯\mathcal{T} under some probability 𝐏\mathbf{P}. We say that the random environment 𝔭\mathfrak{p} satisfies the condition (⋆)𝒯Nq=1,ε(\star)_{\mathcal{T}_{N}}^{q=1,\varepsilon} if the 𝐩v,v∈𝒯\mathbf{p}_{v},v\in\mathcal{T} are independent and if they all almost surely belong to [ε,1−ε][\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]. It turns out that these rather weak requirements are sufficient to preserve the Cardy formula in a random environment.

Theorem 1.10 (Cardy’s formula in random environment).

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and any random environment 𝔭\mathfrak{p} satisfying (⋆)𝒯Nq=1,ε(\star)_{\mathcal{T}_{N}}^{q=1,\varepsilon} one has the following convergence in probability

supx∈[0,1]|ϕ𝒯,𝔭,1​[𝒞⁡([CN;AN],[xN;BN])]−x|→N→∞(ℙ)0.\sup\limits_{x\in[0,1]}\Big|\phi_{\mathcal{T},\mathfrak{p},1}\big[\mathscr{C}([C_{N};A_{N}];[x_{N};B_{N}])\big]-x\Big|\xlongrightarrow[N\to\infty]{(\mathbb{P})}0. (1.16)

In principle, one can try to use the quantitative version of noise sensitivity [35] to obtain explicit speeds of convergence in the previous result. Adapting almost verbatim the proofs of Theorem 1.8 ensures that Theorem 1.10 already holds in the weakly random environment when chosing ε=ε⁡(N)=12−O⁡(log⁡(N)−2)\varepsilon=\varepsilon(N)=\frac{1}{2}-O(\log(N)^{-2}) with polynomial rates of convergence. This Cardy formula in random environment is in sharp contrast with the work of Nolin and Werner [45], which focuses on the deterministic near-critical percolation regime. In that setting, the critical window is given by W(N)=N−3/4+o(1)\textrm{W}(N)=N^{-3/4+o(1)}, and there exists a non-trivial scaling limit where the interface is neither degenerate nor trivial, exhibiting the same Hausdorff dimension 7/47/4 as SLE⁡(6)\mathrm{SLE}(6), yet is not absolutely continuous with respect to SLE⁡(6)\mathrm{SLE}(6). In particular, in the deterministic near-critical setup, the Cardy formula is not true anymore, while the additional layer of randomness in sorting the environment allows to preserve it.

Disclaimer: To the best of our knowledge, we did not find any prior reference to an argument relating the behaviour of the critical random bond percolation and noise sensitivity. In particular, we discovered this argument independently from any external inputs.
