2 A crash introduction into scaling relations

2.1 Recalling scaling relations in the homogenous setup

In this section, we recall in a concise fashion the so-called scaling relations that link the behaviour at large scale of the critical model to properties of the near-critical models. We present here some of the main results of [25] and their counterparts when the bonds of the FK-percolation models are not uniform and translation anymore. We keep the notations of [25]. Before going into precise statements, we recall standard properties of the FK-random cluster models when 1≤q≤41\leq q\leq 4. Let ≤\leq be the partial ordering on edges of {0,1}E\{0,1\}^{E} given by ω≤ω′\omega\leq\omega^{\prime} if and only if for each e∈Ee\in E, ω⁡(e)≤ω′​(e)\omega(e)\leq\omega^{\prime}(e). An event AA is called increasing if for any ω≤ω′\omega\leq\omega^{\prime}, the event ω∈A\omega\in A implies that ω′∈A\omega^{\prime}\in A. Increasing events are those which are preserved when adding open edges to the clusters. Similarly, we say that the boundary condition ξ′\xi^{\prime} dominates the boundary condition ξ\xi if the partition ξ\xi is finer than the partition ξ′\xi^{\prime} (that is to say any wired vertices in ξ\xi are automatically wired in ξ′\xi^{\prime}). This is denoted ξ′≥ξ\xi^{\prime}\geq\xi. The FK-percolation models display some fairly simple properties (that do not require any kind of translation invariance) that we summarise here

  • •

    Positive association For A,BA,B increasing events and ξ\xi a boundary condition,

    ϕG,p¯,qξ​[A∩B]≥ϕG,p¯,qξ​[A]⋅ϕG,p¯,qξ​[B].\phi_{G,\underline{p},q}^{\xi}[A\cap B]\geq\phi_{G,\underline{p},q}^{\xi}[A]\cdot\phi_{G,\underline{p},q}^{\xi}[B]. (2.1)
  • •

    Boundary monotonicity For AA an increasing event and ξ′≥ξ\xi^{\prime}\geq\xi,

    ϕG,p¯,qξ′​[A]≥ϕG,p¯,qξ​[A].\phi_{G,\underline{p},q}^{\xi^{\prime}}[A]\geq\phi_{G,\underline{p},q}^{\xi}[A]. (2.2)
  • •

    Domain Markov property For HH a subgraph of GG and ξ\xi a boundary condition on GG,

    ϕG,p¯,qξ​[ω​ on ​H|ω​ on ​G\H]=ϕH,p¯,qζ​[ω​ on ​H],\phi_{G,\underline{p},q}^{\xi}[\omega\textrm{ on }H|\omega\textrm{ on }G\backslash H]=\phi_{H,\underline{p},q}^{\zeta}[\omega\textrm{ on }H], (2.3)

    where ζ\zeta is the boundary condition on ∂H\partial H induced by wiring vertices together if they are connected in G\HG\backslash H through ω\omega, potentially using connections through ξ\xi.

One on the key tools to understand the role of boundary conditions on events far from the boundary is the so-called mixing rate, which replaces the 44-arm probabilities in Kesten’s original proof of scaling relation for bond percolation [38]. In most notations used until the end of the paper, the parameter 1≤q≤41\leq q\leq 4 is not written in the probabilistic statements to lighten the reading.

Definition 2.1 (Mixing rate- Definition 1.5 in [25]).

For 1<q≤41<q\leq 4, 1≤r≤R1\leq r\leq R, p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) and an edge e0e_{0} incident to the origin, write

Δp​(R):=ϕΛR,p1​[ωe0]−ϕΛR,p0​[ωe0]\Delta_{p}(R):=\phi_{\Lambda_{R},p}^{1}[\omega_{e_{0}}]-\phi_{\Lambda_{R},p}^{0}[\omega_{e_{0}}] (2.4)
Δp​(r,R):=ϕΛR,p1​[𝒞⁡(Λr)]−ϕΛR,p0​[𝒞⁡(Λr)]\Delta_{p}(r,R):=\phi_{\Lambda_{R},p}^{1}[\mathscr{C}(\Lambda_{r})]-\phi_{\Lambda_{R},p}^{0}[\mathscr{C}(\Lambda_{r})] (2.5)

We use the convention that Λ1={e0}\Lambda_{1}=\{e_{0}\} so that for all RR, one has Δp​(R)=Δp​(1,R)\Delta_{p}(R)=\Delta_{p}(1,R). In the uniform deterministic setup, the above quantities are invariant by translation thus defining them for some specific edge around the origin is costless. The following properties of the mixing rate are at the heart of [25]. Recall that for p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), L⁡(p)L(p) is the scale under which the model with parameter pp satisfies RSW. In what follows, d⁡(e,f)d(e,f) denotes the distance between two edges ee and ff.

Theorem 2.2 (Theorem 1.4 and 1.6 in [25]).

Fix 1<q≤41<q\leq 4.

  1. 1.

    For every η<1\eta<1, p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), R≤L⁡(p)R\leq L(p) and every 22 by 11 rectangle ℛ\mathcal{R} containing Λη​R​(e)\Lambda_{\eta R}(e), there exist constants ≍\asymp depending on η\eta such that

    Covp​[ωe,𝒞⁡(ℛ)]≍Δp​(R).\textrm{Cov}_{p}[\omega_{e},\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})]\asymp\Delta_{p}(R). (2.6)
  2. 2.

    (Quasi-multiplicativity) For every p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) and 1≤r≤R≤L⁡(p)1\leq r\leq R\leq L(p),

    Δp​(r)​Δp​(r,R)≍Δp​(R)\Delta_{p}(r)\Delta_{p}(r,R)\asymp\Delta_{p}(R) (2.7)
  3. 3.

    For any two edges e,fe,f such that d⁡(e,f)=R≤L⁡(p)d(e,f)=R\leq L(p),

    Covp​(ωe,ωf)≍Δp​(R)2.\textrm{Cov}_{p}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\asymp\Delta_{p}(R)^{2}. (2.8)

We note that all of the results above rely purely on RSW-type reasoning and estimates, and notably make very limited use of the model’s translation invariance, which we will discuss in more detail in the following section. We now provide a brief explanation of the scaling relation stating that the scaling window for FK-percolation satisfies W​(N)≍(N2​Δpc​(N))−1\textrm{W}(N)\asymp\left(N^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(N)\right)^{-1}. To formulate this in a way more suited to the random bond setting, we work on the torus 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}. In this context, one may still define the mixing rates Δp​(R)\Delta_{p}(R) for R≤NR\leq N, which remain of the same order as in the full-plane case. Indeed, the mixing rates are defined based on measures with free boundary conditions on boxes, which does not depend on whether we are working in the plane or in the torus. In the next theorem and its proof, one sets

W^​(N):=(N2​Δpc​(N))−1\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N):=(N^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(N))^{-1}

to be the “expected value” of the critical window. The following theorem reads as the inequality W​(N)≳W^​(N)\textrm{W}(N)\gtrsim\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N).

Theorem 2.3 (Theorem 1.4 and 1.6 in [25]).

Fix 1<q≤41<q\leq 4, for any N≥1N\geq 1,

  1. 1.

    For every 22 by 11 rectangle ℛ\mathcal{R} in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} of width R≤N/2R\leq N/2 and for every p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) one has

    |ϕ𝕋N,p​[𝒞⁡(ℛ)]−ϕ𝕋N,pc​[𝒞⁡(ℛ)]|≲|p−pc|W^​(N).\Big|\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})]-\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p_{c}}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})]\Big|\lesssim\frac{|p-p_{c}|}{\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N)}. (2.9)
  2. 2.

    (Mixing rates are stable below the characteristic length) There is a small constant c>0c>0 such that |p−pc|≤c⋅W^​(N)|p-p_{c}|\leq c\cdot\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N) and any R≤NR\leq N,

    Δp​(R)≍Δpc​(R),\Delta_{p}(R)\asymp\Delta_{p_{c}}(R), (2.10)

    where the mixing rates are defined for the homogeneous full-plane measure (1.9).

It turns out that this observation is the starting point of many reasonings appearing in the proofs in random environments, as our analysis often boils down to controlling mixing rates there. In this sketch of proof we only focus on the planar supercritical phase p>pcp>p_{c}, the subcritical phase can be treated similarly. Let us explicitly mention that all the ingredients in missing to this sketch are carefully performed in the proofs of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4.

Sketch of proof of Theorem 2.3 when p>pcp>p_{c}.

Let us start by proving the first item, by controlling the rate of growth of its derivative in pp, which reads as (see e.g. [25, (1.11)]

dd​p​ϕ𝕋N,p​[𝒞⁡(ℛ)]=1p⁡(1−p)​∑e∈ENCovp​(𝒞⁡(ℛ),ωe)\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}p}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})]=\frac{1}{p(1-p)}\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p}(\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e}) (2.11)

The analysis in [25, (i) inTheorem 1.6] estimates Covp​(𝒞⁡(ℛ),ωe)\mathrm{Cov}_{p}(\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e}) using the mixing rates Δp\Delta_{p}, via the measure with parameter pp. Here, one wants to make a similar control, but only involving critical mixing rates Δpc\Delta_{p_{c}}. This will involve a circular argument where mixing rates control the rate of growth (with pp) of covariances between edges which control in return the rate of growth (still with pp) of mixing rates. In order to derive some control via Δpc\Delta_{p_{c}} quantities, one possible route is to show that Δp​(R)\Delta_{p}(R) remains comparable (up to constant) to Δpc​(R)\Delta_{p_{c}}(R) when R≤NR\leq N and pp is not too far from pcp_{c}. To carry this analysis, one can first apply the third item of Theorem 2.2 which reads as Δp​(R)≍Covp​(ωe,ωf)\Delta_{p}(R)\asymp\sqrt{\mathrm{Cov}_{p}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})}, where d⁡(e,f)=Rd(e,f)=R. Differentiating this time the edge-covariances one gets

dd​p​Covp​(ωe,ωf)=1p⁡(1−p)​∑g∈ENκ3p​(e,f,g),\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}p}\mathrm{Cov}_{p}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})=\frac{1}{p(1-p)}\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\kappa_{3}^{p}(e,f,g), (2.12)

where the definition of the cumulant κ3p​(e,f,g)\kappa_{3}^{p}(e,f,g) is recalled at the end of Proposition 2.13. Provided the FK measure ϕ𝕋N,p\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p} satisfies some RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) property, one can control each cumulant κ3p​(e,f,g)\kappa_{3}^{p}(e,f,g) using associated mixing rates for the same measure Δp​(⋅)\Delta_{p}(\cdot) as in [25, Proposition 5.6]. Let us now be more concrete about the aforementioned circular reasoning on controlling the whole FK measure when moving it within the critical window. Define the sets of measures on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} whose mixing rates are comparable to the critical ones i.e.

StabΔ(δ,N):={ϕ𝕋N,p|∀R≤N,Δp​(R)Δpc​(R)∈[δ,1/δ]}.\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\delta,N):=\left\{\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p}\Big|\forall R\leq N,\quad\frac{\Delta_{p}(R)}{\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)}\in[\delta,1/\delta]\right\}.

This allows us to define the breaking probability

pb​(δ,N):=inf{p>pc|ϕ𝕋N,p∉RSW​(δ,N)∩StabΔ​(δ,N)}.p_{b}(\delta,N):=\inf\left\{p>p_{c}\Big|\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p}\not\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\cap\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\delta,N)\right\}.

In principle, one should be careful with the choice of a joint δ\delta parameter in RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) and StabΔ​(δ,N)\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\delta,N), as asking for a smaller δ\delta in RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) means that one worsens constants in the estimate Δp​(R)≍Covp​(ωe,ωf)\Delta_{p}(R)\asymp\sqrt{\mathrm{Cov}_{p}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})} and hence one may not be able to show that the stability event StabΔ​(δ,N)\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\delta,N) holds with the same δ\delta. Assume now that one can bypass this difficulty (we refer to the proof of Lemma 3.4 where this is addressed). For any pc≤p≤pb​(δ,N)p_{c}\leq p\leq p_{b}(\delta,N), one can replace, in all the above formulae, the mixing rates for the measure ϕ𝕋N,p\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p} by the critical ones. Using some geometric estimates linking covariances and mixing rates (which are recalled in Section 2.3), one gets, for a 22 by 11 rectangle ℛ\mathcal{R} of width RR and any two edges e,fe,f such that d⁡(e,f)=Rd(e,f)=R,

dd​p​ϕ𝕋N,p​[𝒞⁡(ℛ)]\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}p}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})] ≲R2​Δpc​(R)+∑R<ℓ≤Nℓ​Δpc​(ℓ)​Δpc​(ℓ,R)\displaystyle\lesssim R^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)+\sum_{R<\ell\leq N}\ell\Delta_{p_{c}}(\ell)\Delta_{p_{c}}(\ell,R)
dd​p​Covp​(ωe,ωf)\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}p}\mathrm{Cov}_{p}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f}) ≲Δpc​(R)2​(R2​Δpc​(R)+∑R<ℓ≤Nℓ​Δpc​(ℓ)​Δpc​(ℓ,R)).\displaystyle\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\Bigg(R^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)+\sum_{R<\ell\leq N}\ell\Delta_{p_{c}}(\ell)\Delta_{p_{c}}(\ell,R)\Bigg).

We will see in Remark 2.6 that there exists c=c⁡(q,δ)>0c=c(q,\delta)>0 such that Δpc​(R)≳R2−c\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\gtrsim R^{2-c}. Therefore one gets for pc≤p≤pb​(δ,N)p_{c}\leq p\leq p_{b}(\delta,N)

dd​p​ϕp​[𝒞⁡(ℛ)]\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}p}\phi_{p}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})] ≲N2​Δpc​(N)=W^​(N)−1,\displaystyle\lesssim N^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(N)=\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N)^{-1}, (2.13)
dd​p​Covp​(ωe,ωf)\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}p}\mathrm{Cov}_{p}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f}) ≲Δpc​(R)2⋅N2​Δpc​(N)=Δpc​(R)2​W^​(N)−1.\displaystyle\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\cdot N^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(N)=\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2}\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N)^{-1}. (2.14)

To conclude, one should show that pb​(δ,N)−pc≳W^​(N)p_{b}(\delta,N)-p_{c}\gtrsim\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N). Assuming this fails, there exist a subsequence of NN such that |pb​(δ,N)−pc|=o⁡(W^​(N))|p_{b}(\delta,N)-p_{c}|=o(\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N)). Integrating (2.13) and (2.14) between pcp_{c} and pb​(δ,N)p_{b}(\delta,N), one would have |ϕpb​(δ,N)​[𝒞⁡(ℛ)]−ϕpc​[𝒞⁡(ℛ)]|=o⁡(1)|\phi_{p_{b}(\delta,N)}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})]-\phi_{p_{c}}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})]|=o(1) while dd​p​Covp​(ωe,ωf)=o⁡(Δpc​(R)2)=o⁡(Covpc​(ωe,ωf))\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}p}\mathrm{Cov}_{p}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})=o(\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{2})=o(\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})). Using the fact that crossing probabilities of 22 by 11 rectangles in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} are bounded away from 00 and 11 at pcp_{c}, we get that both crossing probabilities of 22 by 11 rectangles and covariances between edges change by some multiplicative 1+o⁡(1)1+o(1) factor when going from pcp_{c} to pb​(δ,N)p_{b}(\delta,N). For some small enough δ\delta, this will imply that the the measure ϕ𝕋N,pb​(δ,N),q\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p_{b}(\delta,N),q} satisfies RSW​(2​δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N) and StabΔ​(2​δ,N)\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(2\delta,N) (note that for RSW, one actually requires estimates on crossing probabilities with boundary conditions, but we ignore this difficulty here). By continuity in pp all the ϕp​[𝒞​(ℛ)]\phi_{p}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})] and Δp​(R)\Delta_{p}(R) for all the 22 by 11 rectangles ℛ⊂𝕋N\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}, this contradicts the definition of the breaking bond probability pb​(δ,N)p_{b}(\delta,N).

Once we have proven the inequality pb​(δ,N)−pc≳W^​(N)p_{b}(\delta,N)-p_{c}\gtrsim\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N), it is straightforward to conclude the proof of Theorem 2.3. For the first point, if p>pb​(δ,N)p>p_{b}(\delta,N), one crudely bounds |ϕ𝕋N,p​[𝒞⁡(ℛ)]−ϕ𝕋N,pc​[𝒞⁡(ℛ)]|\Big|\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})]-\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},p_{c}}[\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R})]\Big| by 11 and uses the fact that p−pc≳W^​(N)p-p_{c}\gtrsim\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N). If p∈[pc,pb​(δ,N)]{p\in[p_{c},p_{b}(\delta,N)]}, one simply integrates (2.14) between pcp_{c} and pp. For the second point, one may choose cc so that c​W^​(N)≤pb​(δ,N)−pcc\widehat{\textrm{W}}(N)\leq p_{b}(\delta,N)-p_{c}, and then the result comes from integrating equation (2.14) between pcp_{c} and pb​(δ,N)p_{b}(\delta,N), and using the relation between mixing rates and covariances Covp​(ωe,ωf)≍Δp​(d⁡(e,f))2\mathrm{Cov}_{p}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\asymp\Delta_{p}(d(e,f))^{2}.∎

2.2 Scaling relations in non-translation invariant environments

When working with a generic environment p¯=(pe)e∈EN\underline{p}=(p_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}, the obtained probability measures are no longer translation invariant, which creates additional (but in fact limited) complications within the proofs. In our approach focused in keeping some control of the stochastic derivatives of crossing probabilities, mixing rates and arm events, it is necessary to generalise the properties of Theorem 2.2 around each edge ee provided the environment p¯\underline{p} still satisfies RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N). More precisely, for some bond environement p¯=(pe)e∈EN\underline{p}=(p_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}, one can define a local notion of mixing rates around each edge. In what follows, set ΛR​(e):=e+ΛR\Lambda_{R}(e):=e+\Lambda_{R} the translated box of center ee. For e∈𝕋Ne\in\mathbb{T}_{N} and 1≤r≤R≤N/41\leq r\leq R\leq N/4, define

Δp¯(e)​(R):=ϕΛR​(e),p¯,q1​[ωe]−ϕΛR​(e),p¯,q0​[ωe]\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(R):=\phi_{\Lambda_{R}(e),\underline{p},q}^{1}[\omega_{e}]-\phi_{\Lambda_{R}(e),\underline{p},q}^{0}[\omega_{e}] (2.15)
Δp¯(e)​(r,R):=ϕΛR​(e),p¯,q1​[𝒞⁡[Λr​(e)]]−ϕΛR​(e),p¯,q0​[𝒞⁡[Λr​(e)]]\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R):=\phi_{\Lambda_{R}(e),\underline{p},q}^{1}\big[\mathscr{C}[\Lambda_{r}(e)]\big]-\phi_{\Lambda_{R}(e),\underline{p},q}^{0}\big[\mathscr{C}[\Lambda_{r}(e)]\big] (2.16)

The following proposition generalises Theorem 2.2 to non-translation invariant measures that still satisfy some strong box crossing property.

Proposition 2.4.

Assume that the edge weights p¯=(pe)e∈𝕋N\underline{p}=(p_{e})_{e\in\mathbb{T}_{N}} satisfy RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N). In what follows all the constants ≍\asymp depend a priori on the choice of δ\delta.

  1. 1.

    (Mixing-rate/covariance) For any two edges e,f∈𝕋Ne,f\in\mathbb{T}_{N} such that d⁡(e,f)=R<N/4d(e,f)=R<N/4,

    Covp¯​(ωe,ωf)≍Δp¯(e)​(R)​Δp¯(f)​(R).\mathrm{Cov}_{\underline{p}}(\omega_{e},\omega_{f})\asymp\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(R)\Delta^{(f)}_{\underline{p}}(R). (2.17)
  2. 2.

    (Quasimultiplicativity) For any edge e∈𝕋Ne\in\mathbb{T}_{N} any 1≤r<R≤N/41\leq r<R\leq N/4 one has

    Δp¯(e)​(r)​Δp¯(e)​(r,R)≍Δp¯(e)​(R).\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r)\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R)\asymp\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(R). (2.18)
  3. 3.

    (Comparability at small scales) For any two edges e,f∈𝕋Ne,f\in\mathbb{T}_{N} such that d⁡(e,f)≤rd(e,f)\leq r and any 1≤r<R≤N/41\leq r<R\leq N/4, one has

    Δp¯(e)​(r,R)≍Δp¯(f)​(r,R).\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R)\asymp\Delta^{(f)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R). (2.19)

Providing a complete proof of this proposition would require introducing a lot of additional side tools involved in [25], but ending up doing the same proof, almost verbatim. As those statements go beyond the general scope and philosophy of the present paper, we rather provide some intuition on why those results still hold, and then sketch the proof of the second and third item. Fix e∈ENe\in E_{N}, center of the boxes Λr​(e)⊂ΛR​(e)\Lambda_{r}(e)\subset\Lambda_{R}(e) for r≤R≤N/4r\leq R\leq N/4. Assume that on ∂ΛR​(e)\partial\Lambda_{R}(e) one starts with a pair of boundary conditions ξ≤ξ′\xi\leq\xi^{\prime}, such that ξ′\xi^{\prime} is “much more wired” than ξ\xi (this can be formalised rigorously with the notion of boosting pair of boundary conditions in [25, Section 3]). The monotonicity properties of FK-percolation models and the coupling via decision trees allow to couple two configurations ω,ω′\omega,\omega^{\prime} distributed according to ϕΛR,p¯,qξ\phi_{\Lambda_{R},\underline{p},q}^{\xi} and ϕΛR,p¯,qξ′\phi_{\Lambda_{R},\underline{p},q}^{\xi^{\prime}} in such a way that ω≤ω′\omega\leq\omega^{\prime}. Assume we are given such a coupling, one can start by revealing all of the edges in the annulus ΛR​(e)\Λr​(e)\Lambda_{R}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{r}(e) in both ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime}, and read the boundary conditions ζ,ζ′\zeta,\zeta^{\prime} imposed respectively by ω|ΛR(e)\Λr(e),ω′|ΛR(e)\Λr(e)\omega_{|\Lambda_{R}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{r}(e)},\omega^{\prime}_{|\Lambda_{R}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{r}(e)} to ∂Λr​(e)\partial\Lambda_{r}(e). The key feature of the coupling via decision trees studied in [25] reads in the non-translation invariant setup as

Δp¯(e)(r,R)≍ℙ[ζ≠ζ′]≍ℙ[ζ′ is “much more wired than” ζ].\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R)\asymp\mathbb{P}[\zeta\neq\zeta^{\prime}]\asymp\mathbb{P}[\zeta^{\prime}\text{ is ``much more wired than" }\zeta]. (2.20)

The proof of such a statement only requires RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) to transfer information through different scales. Notably, no translation invariance of the model appears within the proofs.

Sketch of the proof of Proposition 2.4 .

Let us start by explaining how the second item follows from (2.20). We do not claim originality here, repeating in a concise way the arguments of [25] providing some intuition to the reader less familiar with the use of mixing rates. The proof of the first item is skipped as it follows the same spirit as the one for the second item, but exploring instead the annuli from inside to outside.

Proof of the second item.

We keep the above setup with ξ=0\xi=0 and ξ′=1\xi^{\prime}=1. In that case, Δp¯(e)​(R)\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(R) is exactly the probability, when coupled in a monotone way (i.e. so that ω′≥ω\omega^{\prime}\geq\omega), that the configurations ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime} do not agree at the edge ee. On the other hand, one can start by revealing all the edges in the annulus ΛR​(e)\Λr​(e)\Lambda_{R}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{r}(e) and obtain boundary conditions ζ,ζ′\zeta,\zeta^{\prime} on ∂Λr​(e)\partial\Lambda_{r}(e). The Domain Markov Property implies that (using here that ω′≥ω\omega^{\prime}\geq\omega)

ℙ[ωe≠ωe′|ζ,ζ′]=ϕΛr​(e),p¯,qζ′[ωe]−ϕΛr​(e),p¯,qζ[ωe].\mathbb{P}[\omega_{e}\neq\omega^{\prime}_{e}|\zeta,\zeta^{\prime}]=\phi_{\Lambda_{r}(e),\underline{p},q}^{\zeta^{\prime}}[\omega_{e}]-\phi_{\Lambda_{r}(e),\underline{p},q}^{\zeta}[\omega_{e}].

The RHS of the above equation vanishes when ζ=ζ′\zeta=\zeta^{\prime}. Assuming that ζ≠ζ′\zeta\neq\zeta^{\prime}, one may use the crude stochastic dominations for 0≤ζ0\leq\zeta and ζ′≤1\zeta^{\prime}\leq 1 to see that for any ζ≤ζ′\zeta\leq\zeta^{\prime},

ℙ[ωe≠ωe′|ζ,ζ′]≤ϕΛr​(e),p¯,q1[ωe]−ϕΛr​(e),p¯,q0[ωe]=Λp¯(e)(r).\mathbb{P}[\omega_{e}\neq\omega^{\prime}_{e}|\zeta,\zeta^{\prime}]\leq\phi_{\Lambda_{r}(e),\underline{p},q}^{1}[\omega_{e}]-\phi_{\Lambda_{r}(e),\underline{p},q}^{0}[\omega_{e}]=\Lambda^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r).

Using that ℙ[ζ≠ζ′]≍Δp¯(e)(r,R)\mathbb{P}[\zeta\neq\zeta^{\prime}]\asymp\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R), one gets a first inequality

Δp¯(e)(R)=ℙ[ωe≠ωe′]≤ℙ[ζ≠ζ′]Δp¯(e)(r)≍Δp¯(e)(r,R)Δp¯(e)(r).\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(R)=\mathbb{P}[\omega_{e}\neq\omega^{\prime}_{e}]\leq\mathbb{P}[\zeta\neq\zeta^{\prime}]\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r)\asymp\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R)\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r).

Let us prove the converse (up to constant) inequality. Assuming that ζ′\zeta^{\prime} is “much more wired” than ζ\zeta, one works for the simplest case where Λ1​(e):={e}\Lambda_{1}(e):=\{e\} and reveal the configurations ω,ω′\omega,\omega^{\prime} in the annulus ΛR​(e)\Λr​(e)\Lambda_{R}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{r}(e). The boundary conditions obtained for ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime} on {e}\{e\} are denoted ζ^,ζ^′\widehat{\zeta},\widehat{\zeta}^{\prime}. For the single edge {e}\{e\}, only the wired and the free boundary conditions are possible. This enforces on the event ζ^≠ζ^′\widehat{\zeta}\neq\widehat{\zeta}^{\prime} that ζ^=0\widehat{\zeta}=0 and ζ^′=1\widehat{\zeta}^{\prime}=1. As a consequence

ℙ[ωe≠ωe′|ζ^,ζ^′]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\big[\omega_{e}\neq\omega^{\prime}_{e}\big|\widehat{\zeta},\widehat{\zeta}^{\prime}\big] =ϕ{e},p¯,q1​[ωe]−ϕ{e},p¯,q0​[ωe]\displaystyle=\phi_{\{e\},\underline{p},q}^{1}[\omega_{e}]-\phi_{\{e\},\underline{p},q}^{0}[\omega_{e}]
=pe−pepe+q⁡(1−pe)≳1,\displaystyle=p_{e}-\frac{p_{e}}{p_{e}+q(1-p_{e})}\gtrsim 1,

where in the inequality, we use q>1q>1 and the fact that the bond parameter pep_{e} is bounded away from 00 and 11 due to the RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) property. Furthermore, on the event EE corresponding to ζ′\zeta^{\prime} being “much more wired” that ζ\zeta, one can apply the reasoning above this proof to the annulus Λr​(e)\Λ1​(e)\Lambda_{r}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{1}(e) which implies that ℙ[ζ^≠ζ^′|ζ,ζ′]≍Δp¯(e)(r)\mathbb{P}\big[\widehat{\zeta}\neq\widehat{\zeta}^{\prime}\big|\zeta,\zeta^{\prime}\big]\asymp\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(e)}(r). All together, this gives

Δp¯(e)(R)=ℙ[ωe≠ωe′]\displaystyle\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(e)}(R)=\mathbb{P}[\omega_{e}\neq\omega_{e}^{\prime}] ≥ℙ⁡[ωe≠ωe′,ζ^≠ζ^′,E]\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{P}\big[\omega_{e}\neq\omega_{e}^{\prime},\widehat{\zeta}\neq\widehat{\zeta}^{\prime},E\big]
=ℙ[ωe≠ωe′|ζ^≠ζ^′,E]⋅ℙ[ζ^≠ζ^′|E]⋅ℙ[E]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\big[\omega_{e}\neq\omega_{e}^{\prime}\big|\widehat{\zeta}\neq\widehat{\zeta}^{\prime},E\big]\cdot\mathbb{P}\big[\widehat{\zeta}\neq\widehat{\zeta}^{\prime}\big|E\big]\cdot\mathbb{P}[E]
≳1⋅Δp¯(e)​(r)⋅Δp¯(e)​(r,R).\displaystyle\gtrsim 1\cdot\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(e)}(r)\cdot\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(e)}(r,R).
Proof of the third item.

The goal here is to prove Δp¯(f)​(r,R)≳Δp¯(e)​(r,R)\Delta^{(f)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R)\gtrsim\Delta^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R), the other inequality follows by symmetry. Notice that one can always assume that R>16​rR>16r, otherwise both terms are uniformly bounded away from 00 and 11 by the RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) property. Consider the annulus A=ΛR​(e)\Λr​(e)A=\Lambda_{R}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{r}(e), which contains the annulus A′=ΛR/2​(f)\Λ2​r​(f)A^{\prime}=\Lambda_{R/2}(f)\backslash\Lambda_{2r}(f) (as d⁡(e,f)≤r≤R/2d(e,f)\leq r\leq R/2). Consider ω≤ω′\omega\leq\omega^{\prime} obtained monotone coupling of the measures ϕΛR​(e),p¯,q1\phi_{\Lambda_{R}(e),\underline{p},q}^{1} and ϕΛR​(e),p¯,q0\phi_{\Lambda_{R}(e),\underline{p},q}^{0}. We reveal successively the edges of AA in both ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime} as follows:

  1. 1.

    First reveal all the edges of ΛR​(e)\ΛR/2​(f)\Lambda_{R}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{R/2}(f), and let ζ1,ζ1′\zeta_{1},\zeta_{1}^{\prime} be the boundary conditions respectively enforced by ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime} on ∂ΛR/2​(f)\partial\Lambda_{R/2}(f).

  2. 2.

    Second, reveal all the edges in A′A^{\prime}, and let ζ2,ζ2′\zeta_{2},\zeta_{2}^{\prime} be the boundary conditions respectively enforced by ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime} on ∂Λ2​r​(f)\partial\Lambda_{2r}(f).

  3. 3.

    Finally, reveal all edges in Λ2​r​(f)\Λr​(e)\Lambda_{2r}(f)\backslash\Lambda_{r}(e), and let ζ3,ζ3′\zeta_{3},\zeta_{3}^{\prime} be the boundary conditions respectively enforced by ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime} on ∂Λr​(e)\partial\Lambda_{r}(e).

The connection between mixing rates and exploration by decision trees (2.20) ensures that Λp¯(e)(r,R)≍ℙ[ζ3≠ζ3′]\Lambda^{(e)}_{\underline{p}}(r,R)\asymp\mathbb{P}[\zeta_{3}\neq\zeta_{3}^{\prime}]. On the other hand, for any ζ1,ζ1′\zeta_{1},\zeta_{1}^{\prime}, monotonicity with respect to boundary conditions gives that

ℙ[ζ2≠ζ2′|ζ1,ζ1′]≤ℙ[ζ2≠ζ2′|ζ1=0,ζ1′=1]≍Δp¯(f)(2r,R/2).\mathbb{P}[\zeta_{2}\neq\zeta_{2}^{\prime}|\zeta_{1},\zeta_{1}^{\prime}]\leq\mathbb{P}[\zeta_{2}\neq\zeta_{2}^{\prime}|\zeta_{1}=0,\zeta_{1}^{\prime}=1]\asymp\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(f)}(2r,R/2).

Notice that if ζ2=ζ2′\zeta_{2}=\zeta_{2}^{\prime}, the configurations ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime} must agree inside Λ2​r​(f)\Lambda_{2r}(f), imposing that ζ3=ζ3′\zeta_{3}=\zeta_{3}^{\prime}. Therefore, un-conditioning the previous equation on ζ1,ζ1′\zeta_{1},\zeta_{1}^{\prime} gives that

Δp¯(e)(r,R)≍ℙ[ζ3≠ζ3′]≤ℙ[ζ2≠ζ2′]≲Δp¯(f)(2r,R/2).\displaystyle\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(e)}(r,R)\asymp\mathbb{P}[\zeta_{3}\neq\zeta_{3}^{\prime}]\leq\mathbb{P}[\zeta_{2}\neq\zeta_{2}^{\prime}]\lesssim\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(f)}(2r,R/2).

Now by quasimultiplicativity which we have just proved above, one may write

Δp¯(f)​(2​r,R/2)≍Δp¯(f)​(r,R)Δp¯(f)​(r,2​r)​Δp¯(f)​(R/2,R)\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(f)}(2r,R/2)\asymp\frac{\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(f)}(r,R)}{\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(f)}(r,2r)\Delta_{\underline{p}}^{(f)}(R/2,R)}

But now some classical RSW estimates allow us to show that for any edge g∈ENg\in E_{N} and ℓ≤N/4\ell\leq N/4, one has Δp¯(g)​(ℓ,2​ℓ)≍1\Delta^{(g)}_{\underline{p}}(\ell,2\ell)\asymp 1, so that putting everything together gives Δ(e)​(r,R)≲Δ(f)​(r,R)\Delta^{(e)}(r,R)\lesssim\Delta^{(f)}(r,R) as desired. ∎

2.3 Geometric estimates on covariances with crossings and arm events

In this section we introduce the notion of arm events, which encode the probability of alternating primal and dual clusters meeting around a point. This notion, which is one of the central objects in the analysis of Kesten’s original proof of scaling relations for Bernoulli percolation, provides some meaningful control on the derivatives of crossing events. Proofs of all of the results in this section can be found in Appendix A.2.

Definition 2.5.

Let e∈ENe\in E_{N} be an edge and fix 1≤r≤R≤N/21\leq r\leq R\leq N/2. One can identify 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} with (ℤ/N​ℤ)2(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{2}, assuming that the image of ee is (0,0)∈(ℤ/N​ℤ)2(0,0)\in(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^{2}. We define the upper half-plane in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} centred at ee as ℍN(e):=(ℤ/N​ℤ)×[0,(N−1)/2]\mathbb{H}^{(e)}_{N}:=(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})\times[0,(N-1)/2]. One can define similarly the lower, left and right half-planes. This allows us to define (see also Figure 2):

  1. 1.

    The 44-arm event 𝒜4(e)​(r,R)\mathcal{A}_{4}^{(e)}(r,R) around ee, which consists of the existence of 44 alternating parity (primal and dual) arms linking ∂Λr​(e)\partial\Lambda_{r}(e) to ∂ΛR​(e)\partial\Lambda_{R}(e) in the annulus ΛR​(e)\Λr​(e)\Lambda_{R}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{r}(e). We denote by π4,p¯(e)​(r,R)\pi_{4,\underline{p}}^{(e)}(r,R) the probability of this event under ϕ𝕋N,p¯\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p}}.

  2. 2.

    The upper half-plane three-arm event 𝒜3+(e)​(r,R)\mathcal{A}_{3^{+}}^{(e)}(r,R) around ee, which consists of to the existence of 33 alternating parity (22 primal and 11 dual) arms linking ∂Λr​(e)\partial\Lambda_{r}(e) to ∂ΛR​(e)\partial\Lambda_{R}(e) inside the half- annulus ΛR​(e)\Λr​(e)∩ℍN(e)\Lambda_{R}(e)\backslash\Lambda_{r}(e)\cap\mathbb{H}^{(e)}_{N}. We denote by π3+,p¯(e)​(r,R)\pi_{3^{+},\underline{p}}^{(e)}(r,R) the probability of this event under ϕ𝕋N,p¯\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\underline{p}}. One can define similarly the lower, right and left half-plane three arm events denoted respectively 𝒜3−(e)​(r,R),𝒜3rg(e)​(r,R)\mathcal{A}_{3^{-}}^{(e)}(r,R),\mathcal{A}_{3^{\textrm{rg}}}^{(e)}(r,R) and 𝒜3lf(e)​(r,R)\mathcal{A}_{3^{\textrm{lf}}}^{(e)}(r,R).

Remark 2.6.

At criticality, the probabilities of the arm events no longer depend on the edge ee so we remove it from the notation, and one can estimate the aforementioned arm events uniformly in r≤R≤N/2r\leq R\leq N/2. There exist constants ≲,≍\lesssim,\asymp and c>0c>0, only depending on δ\delta such that

  1. (i)

    π4,pc​(r,R)≲(r/R)c​Δpc​(r,R)\pi_{4,p_{c}}(r,R)\lesssim(r/R)^{c}\Delta_{p_{c}}(r,R),

  2. (ii)

    π3+,pc​(r,R)≍(r/R)2\pi_{3^{+},p_{c}}(r,R)\asymp(r/R)^{2},

  3. (iii)

    (r/R)c≳Δpc​(r,R)≳(r/R)2−c(r/R)^{c}\gtrsim\Delta_{p_{c}}(r,R)\gtrsim(r/R)^{2-c},

  4. (iv)

    For q=1q=1, (r/R)1+c≳π4,pc​(r,R)≳(r/R)2−c(r/R)^{1+c}\gtrsim\pi_{4,p_{c}}(r,R)\gtrsim(r/R)^{2-c}.

The first and third items are proved in [25, Theorem 1.6 (iv), Proposition 1.8] and the second item is proved in [26, Proposition 6.6 (6.7)] for q<4q<4, but the proof adapts verbatim for q=4q=4. The fourth item reads as the fact that the four-arm exponent α4\alpha_{4} is strictly bigger than 11 and strictly smaller than 22 for percolation. The upper bound has been proven by different means (see e.g. [12] for an extensive exposition) while the upper bound is proven in [26, Proposition 6.8] for example.

In this section we present, in the simplified critical setup at pcp_{c}, one additional technicality that appears in the computations in non-translation invariant random environments. Namely, it will be crucial to estimate the sum of squares of covariances between an edge and a crossing (this is in contrast with [25] where it is enough to control the sum of covariances to run the proofs). Let us start by presenting more precise estimates regarding the covariances between an edge some crossing events.

Lemma 2.7.

Let R≤N/2R\leq N/2, ℛ\mathcal{R} be a 22 by 11 rectangle of width RR and e∈ENe\in E_{N}. Then one can estimate Covpc​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e}) by:

  • •

    If dist​(e,ℛ)=ℓ≥R\textrm{dist}(e,\mathcal{R})=\ell\geq R one has

    Covpc​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)≍Δpc​(R,ℓ)​Δpc​(ℓ)\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\asymp\Delta_{p_{c}}(R,\ell)\Delta_{p_{c}}(\ell)
  • •

    If the distance from ee to of the four corners of ℛ\mathcal{R} is n≲Rn\lesssim R, one has

    Covpc​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)≲Δpc​(n).\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\lesssim\Delta_{p_{c}}(n).

A similar estimate holds for arbitrary boundary conditions as well as dual crossings.

The proof of this lemma, which is key to deduce stability of arm events in non-translation invariant environments, is delayed to Appendix A.2. Let us still mention that in the second case, the correct upper bound should be of order Δpc​(R)\Delta_{p_{c}}(R), but proving this requires better estimates on certain arm events than one could get from RSW alone.

Remark 2.8.

Under the previous assumptions, one has

∑e∈ENCovpc​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)\displaystyle\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e}) ≲∑R<r≤Nr​Δpc​(R,r)​Δpc​(r)+∑r≤Rr​Δpc​(r)\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{R<r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(R,r)\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)+\sum_{r\leq R}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r) (2.21)
≲∑r≤Nr​Δpc​(r)≍W​(N)−1\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)\asymp\textrm{W}(N)^{-1} (2.22)

and

∑e∈ENCovpc​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)2\displaystyle\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2} ≲∑R<r≤Nr​Δpc​(R,r)2​Δpc​(r)2+∑r≤Rr​Δpc​(r)2\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{R<r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(R,r)^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}+\sum_{r\leq R}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2} (2.23)
≲∑r≤Nr​Δpc​(r)2=Ξ​(N)−1,\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}=\Xi(N)^{-1}, (2.24)

where we recall the definition Ξ⁡(N)=(∑r≤Nr​Δpc​(r)2)−1\Xi(N)=\big(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}\big)^{-1}.

We now some analogous statement for covariances between edges and arm events.

Lemma 2.9.

Let e,f∈𝕋Ne,f\in\mathbb{T}_{N} and R≤N/2R\leq N/2. Then for #∈{4,3+,3−,3rg,3lf}\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}, one has

Covpc​(𝒜#(e)​(R),ωf)≲π#​(R)​Δpc​(n),\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathcal{A}_{\#}^{(e)}(R),\omega_{f})\lesssim\pi_{\#}(R)\Delta_{p_{c}}(n),

where nn is the minimal distance from ff to either ee or one of the bottom corners of ΛR​(e)∩ℍN(e)\Lambda_{R}(e)\cap\mathbb{H}^{(e)}_{N}.

Remark 2.10.

Summing Lemma 2.9 over edges in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} one gets for any e∈ENe\in E_{N} and 1≤R≤N/21\leq R\leq N/2,

∑f∈ECovpc​(𝒜#(e)​(R),ωf)\displaystyle\sum_{f\in E}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathcal{A}_{\#}^{(e)}(R),\omega_{f}) ≲π#,pc​(R)​∑r≤Nr​Δpc​(r)≍π#,pc​(R)​W​(N)−1\displaystyle\lesssim\pi_{\#,p_{c}}(R)\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)\asymp\pi_{\#,p_{c}}(R)\textrm{W}(N)^{-1} (2.25)
∑f∈ECovpc​(𝒜#(e)​(R),ωf)2\displaystyle\sum_{f\in E}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathcal{A}_{\#}^{(e)}(R),\omega_{f})^{2} ≲π#,pc​(R)2​∑r≤Nr​Δpc​(r)2=π#,pc​(R)2​Ξ​(N)−1.\displaystyle\lesssim\pi_{\#,p_{c}}(R)^{2}\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2}=\pi_{\#,p_{c}}(R)^{2}\Xi(N)^{-1}. (2.26)

All of the previous results are valid for 1<q≤41<q\leq 4. For q=1q=1, we may also get similar estimates by replacing mixing rates by four-arm events. We note that in this case, the fourth item of Remark 2.6 allows us to show that Ξ⁡(N)\Xi(N) is of constant order.

Lemma 2.11.

Assume that q=1q=1, and that we are at pc​(1)=12p_{c}(1)=\frac{1}{2}. Then all of the results of Lemmas 2.7 and 2.9, as well as the computations that follow in Remarks 2.8 and 2.10 still hold, when replacing all mixing rates Δpc​(r,R)\Delta_{p_{c}}(r,R) by four-arm events π4,pc​(r,R)\pi_{4,p_{c}}(r,R). Furthermore, in the computations in the remarks, one may replace Ξ⁡(N)\Xi(N) by 11.

The quantity Ξ⁡(N)\Xi(N) will appear numerous times throughout the paper, so we would like to relate it to the critical window W​(N)\textrm{W}(N). We show a slightly stronger result which will be useful to us later. Recall that W~​(N)\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N) is the modified critical window, given by

W~(N)=W(N)(∑r≤NrΔpc(r)4)−1/2.\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)=\textrm{W}(N)\left(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\right)^{-1/2}.

W​(N)​Nc≲W~​(N)2/3≲Ξ⁡(N).\textrm{W}(N)N^{c}\lesssim\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{2/3}\lesssim\Xi(N).

2.4 Derivatives of events for non-translation invariant environments

The overall approach that we take in the present paper is to deform continuously, via a continuous family of bonds 𝔭⁡(s)\mathfrak{p}(s), all the edge weights from the critical homogeneous setup at pcp_{c} towards the set of weights 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. In the deterministic setup, at criticality and below the characteristic length, the strong box-crossing property allows us to deduce all relations recalled inside Theorems 2.2 and 2.3. As time evolves along the deformation process, the fact that some RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) property remains true (with high probability) for the set of weights 𝔭⁡(s)\mathfrak{p}(s) ensures that Proposition 2.4 remains true for the weights 𝔭⁡(s)\mathfrak{p}(s) and with all involved quantities remaining the same as the homogeneous ones up to multiplicative constant. Therefore, one can run some infinitesimal deformation from the weights 𝔭⁡(s)\mathfrak{p}(s) to 𝔭⁡(s+d​s)\mathfrak{p}(s+ds), which implies in return that RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) holds at time s+d​ss+ds, implying in return Proposition 2.4 for the weights 𝔭⁡(s+d​s)\mathfrak{p}(s+ds).

One can now compute explicitly the derivatives of different quantities with respect to each edge bond pep_{e}. The proof of the following proposition is given in Appendix A.1.

3 Near-critical random bond FK-percolation for naively centered random variables

3.1 Gaussian variables centred at pc​(q)p_{c}(q)

3.1.1 Statement of the result and setup of the proof

Throughout this section, we fix some 1<q≤41<q\leq 4, and drop the dependencies in qq from our notations. We start by proving Theorem 1.5 in the special case of a sequence of i.i.d. Gaussian variables whose law is given by

𝐩e​=(d)​𝒩​(pc​(q),σN2),\mathbf{p}_{e}\overset{(d)}{=}\mathcal{N}(p_{c}(q),\sigma_{N}^{2}), (3.1)

where the parameter σN\sigma_{N} goes to 00 as the size of 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} goes to infinity. Note that the probability that a given 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} stays in the interval [0,1][0,1] is at most ≲exp(−c⋅σN−2)\lesssim\exp(-c\cdot\sigma_{N}^{-2}) for some universal constant c>0c>0. In practice, σN\sigma_{N} will be chosen to decay polynomially fast in NN, implying, by a straightforward union bound, that all the bond parameters 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈EN\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} belong to [0,1][0,1] with high probability, making the FK measures ϕ𝕋N,𝔭\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}} well defined. The special role given in our analysis of the case of i.i.d. Gaussian variables is related to the so-called Skorokhod embedding theorem, which informally states that any centred random variable with regular enough integrability properties and tails can indeed be realised as some Brownian motion stopped at some well chosen stopping time. As a toy example in our analysis, we present a simplified proof of Theorem 1.5 when the random environment 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} is given by (3.1), as it will be a first incremental step to introduce the core arguments necessary to work both for random variables satisfying either (⋆)NA(\star)^{\text{A}}_{N} or (⋆)NB(\star)^{\text{B}}_{N}. This reads in the following proposition.

Proposition 3.1.

Assume that the random environment 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈EN\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} under 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} is given by i.i.d Gaussians satisfying (3.1) for some uniform parameter σN\sigma_{N}. Then there exists δ=δ⁡(q)>0\delta=\delta(q)>0 and some positive constants c=c⁡(q,δ)c=c(q,\delta), O=O⁡(q,δ)O=O(q,\delta) such that for any N≥1N\geq 1 and any σN≤c⋅W​(N)1/2\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}, one has

𝐏N[ϕ𝕋N,𝔭∈RSW(δ,N)]≥1−O(exp[−cNc(W​(N)1/2σN)2]).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\Bigg(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\sigma_{N}}\Bigg)^{2}\Bigg]\Bigg).

Before diving into the proof, let us introduce additional notations, and highlight pieces of the strategy we use. As aforementioned, rather than directly looking at the FK measure with bonds parameters given by (𝐩e)e∈EN(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}, we introduce a time indexed continuous family of FK measures, starting at the homogeneous critical setup and ending at (𝐩e)e∈EN(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}}. More precisely, for any t≥0t\geq 0, define the process 𝔭⁡(t):=(𝐩e​(t))e∈EN\mathfrak{p}(t):=(\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}, whose components are mutually independent and given by

𝐩e​(t):=pc​(q)+Bt(e),\mathbf{p}_{e}(t):=p_{c}(q)+B^{(e)}_{t},

where for each e∈ENe\in E_{N}, t↦Bt(e)t\mapsto B^{(e)}_{t} is a standard Brownian motion attached to the edge ee. One defines the natural (completed) filtration ℱtN:=σ⁡((Bs(e))0≤s≤t,e∈EN)\mathcal{F}^{N}_{t}:=\sigma((B^{(e)}_{s})_{0\leq s\leq t},e\in E_{N}), and by abuse of notation, also write 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} for the probability measure associated to the Brownian motions. It is straightforward to see that 𝔭⁡(0)=(pc)e∈EN\mathfrak{p}(0)=(p_{c})_{e\in E_{N}} and that t↦𝔭⁡(t)t\mapsto\mathfrak{p}(t) is 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}-almost surely continuous with 𝔭⁡(σN2)=(d)𝔭\mathfrak{p}(\sigma_{N}^{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\mathfrak{p}. To prove Proposition 3.1, we will show that for t≲W​(N)t\lesssim\textrm{W}(N), all the measures s↦(ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(s),q)s≤ts\mapsto(\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s),q})_{s\leq t} remain within the RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) class, at least with high 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}-probability. For the sake of notations, we will couple the evolving environment 𝔭⁡(t)\mathfrak{p}(t) with 𝔭\mathfrak{p} so that 𝔭⁡(σN2)=𝔭\mathfrak{p}(\sigma_{N}^{2})=\mathfrak{p}, that is to say for each ee, one has 𝐩e​(σN2)=𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e}(\sigma_{N}^{2})=\mathbf{p}_{e}. Our strategy enhances the ideas present in the original proof of Theorem 2.3 to our random context. More practically, this means keeping track along the time deformation of the stability of the RSW box crossing property, the mixing rates and the arm exponents everywhere in ENE_{N}. Some circular argument appears, as the crossing probabilities in rectangles and the arm exponents control the time dependent stochastic derivatives of the mixing rates, which control in return the time derivatives of the crossing probabilities and arm exponents. The overall interplay between those quantities will allow the FK measures to stay resembling the critical one.

Set two positive parameters δ,ρ\delta,\rho whose value will be fixed through the proof, and will in fact only depend on 1<q≤41<q\leq 4. In particular, all the constants ≲,≍\lesssim,\asymp will depend depend on δ\delta and ρ\rho (thus on qq), except within the proof of Lemma 3.4 where the dependency will be explicited. In order to quantify the fact that the FK model with parameters 𝔭⁡(t)\mathfrak{p}(t) deviates too much from the critical one, we introduce some breaking time Tb​(δ,ρ)T_{b}(\delta,\rho), where the model no longer exhibits critical behavior, in the spirit of the deterministic breaking point pbp_{b} introduced in the proof of Theorem 2.3. More precisely, the random variable Tb​(δ,ρ)T_{b}(\delta,\rho) is the stopping time for the filtration ℱtN\mathcal{F}^{N}_{t} corresponding to the first instant that 𝔭⁡(t)\mathfrak{p}(t) no longer satisfies at least one of the stability conditions discussed in Section 2.5, i.e.

Tb=Tb​(δ,ρ):=inf{t≥0|ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)∉RSW​(δ,N)∩(⋂#Stab#​(δ,N))∩StabΔ​(ρ,N)}T_{b}=T_{b}(\delta,\rho):=\inf\left\{t\geq 0\Bigg|\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}\not\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\cap\left(\bigcap_{\#}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(\delta,N)\right)\cap\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\rho,N)\right\}

where the indices #\# run through {4,3+,3−,3rg,3lf}\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}. Note that the Δ\Delta (mixing rates) stability involves some constant ρ\rho instead of δ\delta, which is a priori different, and will be fixed during the proofs. Requiring the strong box-crossing property at each scale RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) enforces (for a box of size 11) that all the edges in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} are open with probability between δ\delta and 1−δ1-\delta. As a consequence, for any 0≤t≤Tb​(δ,ρ)0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho), all of the bond parameters 𝐩e​(t)\mathbf{p}_{e}(t) remain bounded away from 00 and 11, making sense of the measure ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)} up to time Tb​(δ,ρ)T_{b}(\delta,\rho). Using the very definition of Tb​(δ,ρ)T_{b}(\delta,\rho), one can see Proposition 3.1 as a consequence of the fact that, with high 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} probability, the breaking time Tb​(δ,ρ)T_{b}(\delta,\rho) is not too small. In fact, it will suffice to show that there exist constants δ,ρ,c,≲\delta,\rho,c,\lesssim such that for all σN≤c⋅W​(N)1/2\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2},

𝐏[Tb(δ,ρ)<σN2]≲exp[−cNc(W​(N)1/2σN)2].\mathbf{P}\Big[T_{b}(\delta,\rho)<\sigma_{N}^{2}\Big]\lesssim\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\left(\frac{\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}}{\sigma_{N}}\right)^{2}\Bigg]. (3.2)

Once Proposition 3.1 is related to the probability that TbT_{b} is not too small, the proof goes via proving that probabilities of crossing events of the form ϕℛ′,𝔭⁡(t),q0​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)]\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathfrak{p}(t),q}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})] (similar to those introduced in Definition 1.4), mixing rates, and probabilities of arm events, do not deviate too much from their original value critical value 𝔭⁡(0)\mathfrak{p}(0). One (small) subtlety when applying standard FK percolation arguments relating different scales is the influence of boundary conditions on mixing (notably those on ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} when considering the crossings of ℛ\mathcal{R}). In order to sidestep this problem, one can consider some slightly more evolved crossing events, in the spirit of the properties involved in Definition RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)

Definition 3.2.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be a 22 by 11 rectangle of width R≤N/8R\leq N/8 in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}, and let ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime} be the rectangle with the same center as ℛ\mathcal{R} but twice larger side lengths. Define 𝒞⁡(ℛ′\ℛ)\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R}) (respectively 𝒞⋆​(ℛ′\ℛ)\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})) to be the event that there exists a primal (respectively a dual) circuit inside the annulus ℛ′\ℛ\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R} and separating the outer boundaries of ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}. We can then define the modified crossing events by setting, for ∙∈{h,v}\bullet\in\{h,v\} (see Figure 3 for an illustration)

{𝒞∙0​(ℛ):=𝒞∙​(ℛ)∩𝒞⋆​(ℛ′\ℛ),𝒞∙⋆1​(ℛ):=𝒞∙⋆​(ℛ)∩𝒞⁡(ℛ′\ℛ).\begin{cases}\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{0}(\mathcal{R})&:=\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})\cap\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R}),\\ \mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star 1}(\mathcal{R})&:=\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star}(\mathcal{R})\cap\mathscr{C}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R}).\\ \end{cases}

Standard conditioning and monotonicity arguments ensure that, for any 𝔭\mathfrak{p} and any ∙∈{h,v}\bullet\in\{h,v\} one has

ϕ𝕋N,𝔭​[𝒞∙0​(ℛ)]≤ϕ𝕋N,𝔭​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)|𝒞⋆​(ℛ′\ℛ)].\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\leq\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})|\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})].

Conditionally on the event 𝒞⋆​(ℛ′\ℛ)\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R}), one can explore the FK clusters from ∂ℛ′\partial\mathcal{R}^{\prime} inwards, until finding a dual path circulating the annulus ℛ′\ℛ\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R}. A piece of this path can be seen as the boundary of some domain simply connected domain 𝒟\mathcal{D}, which hasn’t been explored and contains ℛ\mathcal{R} as a sub-domain (see Figure 3). The dual-connected boundary corresponds to free boundary conditions on 𝒟\mathcal{D}, which implies via the domain Markov property that

ϕ𝕋N,𝔭​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)|𝒞⋆​(ℛ′\ℛ)]=ϕ𝕋N,𝔭​[ϕ𝒟,𝔭0​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)]|𝒞⋆​(ℛ′\ℛ)].\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})|\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})]=\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}\Big[\phi_{\mathcal{D},\mathfrak{p}}^{0}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\Big|\mathscr{C}^{\star}(\mathcal{R}^{\prime}\backslash\mathcal{R})\Big].

As the event 𝒞∙​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}) is increasing, domain monotonicity ensures that for all domains 𝒟\mathcal{D} contained in ℛ′\mathcal{R}^{\prime}, one has ϕ𝒟,𝔭0​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)]≤ϕℛ′,𝔭0​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)]\phi_{\mathcal{D},\mathfrak{p}}^{0}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]\leq\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]. Putting everything together gives

ϕ𝕋N,𝔭​[𝒞∙0​(ℛ)]≤ϕℛ′,𝔭0​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)].\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{0}(\mathcal{R})]\leq\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})].

A similar analysis for the dual model ensures that for any 𝔭\mathfrak{p} and ∙∈{h,v}\bullet\in\{h,v\} one has

ϕ𝕋N,𝔭​[𝒞∙⋆1​(ℛ)]≤ϕℛ′,𝔭1​[𝒞∙⋆​(ℛ)].\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star 1}(\mathcal{R})]\leq\phi^{1}_{\mathcal{R}^{\prime},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}^{\star}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})].

Therefore, if one wants to check the RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) property on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}, it is enough to check that the both probabilities of the events 𝒞∙0​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{0}(\mathcal{R}) and 𝒞∙⋆1​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star 1}(\mathcal{R}) remain are larger (or equal to) than δ\delta. In particular, one can restrict the analysis to events for the full torus measure ϕ𝕋N,𝔭\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}, not involving boundary conditions in sub-domains. Let us add that, conversely, standard RSW theory ensures that provided the measure ϕ𝕋N,𝔭\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}} satisfies RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N), then both lower bounds ϕ𝕋N,𝔭​[𝒞∙0​(ℛ)]≥δ′\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{0}(\mathcal{R})]\geq\delta^{\prime} and ϕ𝕋N,𝔭​[𝒞∙⋆1​(ℛ)]≥δ′\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}^{\star 1}(\mathcal{R})]\geq\delta^{\prime} hold for some δ′>0\delta^{\prime}>0 only depending on δ\delta.

3.1.2 Proving stability of the FK measures below TbT_{b}

One can now pass to the core of the proof, based on the following two lemmas, that evaluate how crossing probabilities, arm events and mixing rates evolve when 𝔭⁡(t)\mathfrak{p}(t) moves from the uniform measure 𝔭⁡(0)\mathfrak{p}(0). All the crossing event derivatives with respect to some specific edge-weight pep_{e} are recalled in Section 2.4. Hence, it remains to apply the Itô’s formula and estimate the order of magnitude of each term involved. In order to obtain δ\delta-dependent absolute constants, one should enforce in the reasonings presented below the possibility to chose constants only depending on δ\delta (and in particular ρ=ρ⁡(δ)\rho=\rho(\delta)) provided δ\delta is small enough. In the proof of lemma 3.4, we explicitly adopt the ≍ρ,δ,≲ρ,δ\asymp_{\rho,\delta},\lesssim_{\rho,\delta} convention (and similarly when constants only depend on δ\delta or ρ\rho) to make the logic more transparent.

Lemma 3.3.

Assume that δ\delta is chosen small enough, only depending on 1<q≤41<q\leq 4. Then for all ρ>0\rho>0, there are some positive constants c=c⁡(δ,ρ,q)>0c=c(\delta,\rho,q)>0 and Oδ,ρ​(⋅)O_{\delta,\rho}(\cdot) such that if σN2≤c⋅W​(N)\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N), one has

𝐏N[∀ 0≤s≤(σN2∧Tb(δ,ρ)), ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(s)∈RSW(2δ,N)]≥1−Oδ,ρ(exp[−cNcW​(N)σN2]).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\textrm{ }0\leq s\leq\Big(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)\Big),\textrm{ }\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta,\rho}\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg]\Bigg).

Moreover, the same statement holds when replacing RSW​(2​δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N) by Stab#​(2​δ,N)\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(2\delta,N) for any #∈{4,3+,3−,3rg,3lf}\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}.

Lemma 3.4.

Assume that δ>0\delta>0 is arbitrary. Then there exists a constant ρ=ρ⁡(δ)>0\rho=\rho(\delta)>0 small enough and constants c=c⁡(δ,q)>0c=c(\delta,q)>0 and Oδ​(⋅)O_{\delta}(\cdot) such that if σN2≤c⋅W​(N)\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c\cdot\textrm{W}(N), one has

𝐏N[∀0≤s≤(σN2∧Tb(δ,ρ)),ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(s)∈StabΔ(2ρ,N)]≥1−Oδ(exp[−cNcW​(N)σN2]).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall~~0\leq s\leq\Big(\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho)\Big),\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(2\rho,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta}\Bigg(\exp\Bigg[-cN^{c}\frac{\textrm{W}(N)}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\Bigg]\Bigg).

Let us comment on the asymmetry of the statements in these two lemmas. The stability event StabΔ​(ρ,N)\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\rho,N) estimates the mixing rates Δ𝔭⁡(t)(e)​(R)\Delta_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}^{(e)}(R), while those mixing rates are only used in computations up to multiplicative constants coming from the RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) bounds. Therefore, picking a smaller δ\delta in the RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) bounds worsens the bounds the mixing rates, which implies that one should in return change ρ\rho in order show that the FK measures still belong to the StabΔ​(ρ,N)\textrm{Stab}_{\Delta}(\rho,N) class. To conclude the proof of Proposition 3.1, one needs to make a joint choice of δ\delta and ρ\rho. One first picks δ\delta according to Lemma 3.3, and then selects ρ\rho according to Lemma 3.4 according to δ\delta. We now pass to the proof of the aforementioned lemmas, starting with Lemma 3.3, using the Itô formula to bound stochastic derivatives in the random environment.

Proof of Lemma 3.3.

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be any event defined on 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}. Since the standard Brownian motions ((Bt(e))t≥0)e∈EN\big((B^{(e)}_{t})_{t\geq 0}\big)_{e\in E_{N}} are i.i.d , one can apply the Itô lemma which reads as

where the d\mathrm{d} operator corresponds to the standard stochastic differentiation. Plugging the explicit formulae obtained in Proposition 2.13 one gets

+∑e∈EN1𝐩e​(t)​(1−𝐩e​(t))2(1−1𝐩e​(t)ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)[ωe])Cov𝔭⁡(t)(𝒮,ωe)dt.\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]\right)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathcal{S},\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t.

We are going to evaluate the order of magnitude of the two previous lines for times 0≤t≤Tb​(δ,ρ)0\leq t\leq T_{b}(\delta,\rho) for the special case of the events 𝒮=𝒞∙0​(ℛ)\mathcal{S}=\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}) or 𝒮=𝒞∙⋆1​(ℛ)\mathcal{S}=\mathscr{C}^{\star 1}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}). One of the takeaway points of [25] is the possibility, at and near criticality, to express event covariances and edge-influences only using mixing rates Δ\Delta. Below the breaking time Tb​(δ,ρ)T_{b}(\delta,\rho), all the mixing rates remain comparable up to constant to the critical ones Δpc\Delta_{p_{c}}, whose analysis in [25] was recalled in Section 2.5. We only work out the details when 𝒮=𝒞∙0​(ℛ)\mathcal{S}=\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}), the case 𝒮=𝒞∙⋆1​(ℛ)\mathcal{S}=\mathscr{C}^{\star 1}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}) can be treated similarly. The cases ∙=h\bullet=h and ∙=v\bullet=v are exactly identical so we just write ∙\bullet for the proof.

    The complement of the event inside 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} in the above equation is the event that for any 0≤s≤σN2∧Tb​(δ,ρ)0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b}(\delta,\rho) and any 22 by 11 rectangle ℛ⊂𝕋N\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{T}_{N}, the probability of any primal crossing ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(s)​[𝒞∙0​(ℛ)]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}[\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})] is at least 2​δ2\delta. Adapting the proof for arm events.

When proving the stability of the arm events 𝒜#(e)​(R)\mathcal{A}^{(e)}_{\#}(R), one can run almost verbatim the proof made for the crossing event 𝒞∙0​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}), replacing (2.22) and (2.24) by respectively (2.25) and (2.26). In this case, the probabilities of arm events ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)​[𝒜#(e)​(R)]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{A}^{(e)}_{\#}(R)] are not bounded away from 00 and 11 uniformly in NN, so one needs to keep track of the additional pre-factors π#,pc​(R)\pi_{\#,p_{c}}(R) that appear in front of the stochastic derivatives, exactly as in Remark 2.10. ∎ We prove now Lemma 3.4 with very similar methods, using a slightly more delicate strategy due when controlling the covariances between multiple edges.

3.2 General random variables satisfying (⋆)NA(\star)^{\textmd{A}}_{N}

In Section 3.1, we proved Theorem 1.5 in the specific case when the random bond parameters are independent Gaussians with a common variance. The role of the present section is to explain how one can extend the proof of this result to a sequence of variables (𝐩e)e∈EN(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} satisfying the condition (⋆)NA(\star)^{\text{A}}_{N}. Recall that at each edge e∈ENe\in E_{N}, the random variable 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} has standard deviation σe:=𝔼​[(𝐩e−pc)2]1/2\sigma_{e}:=\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c})^{2}]^{1/2}. Ideally, one would like to apply exactly the same reasoning as the Gaussian case, by continuously moving the bond parameters from the uniform critical parameter pc​(q)p_{c}(q) towards 𝔭=(𝐩e)e\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e} via some continuous process 𝔭⁡(t)=(𝐩e​(t))e∈EN\mathfrak{p}(t)=(\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}. In fact, we would like this continuous process to resemble independent Brownian motions, allowing us to repeat the technology developed in Section 3.1. This ideal setup can in fact be achieved by the famous Skorokhod embedding theorem, that allows to rewrite any reasonable centred random variable as some Brownian motion stopped appropriately. This reads in the following theorem.

Theorem 3.5 (Skorokhod embedding theorem).

Let XX be a centred real value random variable with a finite second moment. Let (Bt)t≥0(B_{t})_{t\geq 0} a standard Brownian motion for some (completed) filtration (ℱt)t≥0(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}. Then there exist some stopping time TT for the filtration (ℱt)t≥0(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0} such that

BT=(d)X,𝔼⁡[T]=𝔼⁡[X2].\begin{array}[]{rcl}B_{T}&\overset{(d)}{=}&X,\\ \mathbb{E}[T]&=&\mathbb{E}[X^{2}].\end{array}

We now explain how to implement the Skorokhod embedding theorem in the context of the random bond measure 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. There exist a sequence of independent Brownian motions ((Bt(e))t≥0)e∈EN\big((B_{t}^{(e)})_{t\geq 0}\big)_{e\in E_{N}} for some probability measure ℙ\mathbb{P} and a sequence of associated stopping times (T(e))e∈EN\big(T^{(e)}\big)_{e\in E_{N}} for the Brownian motions ((Bt(e))t≥0)e∈EN\big((B_{t}^{(e)})_{t\geq 0}\big)_{e\in E_{N}}, such that for each edge e∈ENe\in E_{N}, the variable pc+BT(e)(e)p_{c}+B^{(e)}_{T^{(e)}} has the law of 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e}. One can set

𝐩e​(t):=pc​(q)+Bt∧T(e)(e).\mathbf{p}_{e}(t):=p_{c}(q)+B^{(e)}_{t\wedge T^{(e)}}. (3.12)

The stopping times T(e)T^{(e)} coming from Skorokhod’s embedding theorem are almost surely finite, which implies that almost surely (with respect to the randomness of the Brownian motions) one has 𝐩e​(∞)=(d)𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e}(\infty)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\mathbf{p}_{e}. To simplify readability, couple the process 𝔭⁡(t)\mathfrak{p}(t) to the random environment 𝔭\mathfrak{p} so that this equality in distribution as an equality.

The stopping times given by the Skorokhod embedding theorem are a priori not unique, and we present here a construction that gives a stopping time with good tails estimates. The following technical lemma is proven in the Appendix via Lemma B.1.

Lemma 3.6.

Let XX be a random variable with stretched exponential tails

ℙ[X>t]≲exp(−ctγ)\mathbb{P}[X>t]\lesssim\exp(-ct^{\gamma})

for some positive constants ≲,c,γ\lesssim,c,\gamma. Let (Bt)t≥0(B_{t})_{t\geq 0} be a standard Brownian motion for the filtration (ℱt)t≥0(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}. Then there exists a stopping time TT, for the filtration (ℱt)t≥0(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\geq 0}, that satisfies the Skorokhod embedding Theorem and such that

ℙ[T>t]≲exp(−c′tγγ+2)\mathbb{P}[T>t]\lesssim\exp\left(-c^{\prime}t^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\right)

for some positive constants ≲,c′\lesssim,c^{\prime} only depending on cc and γ\gamma.

Applying this result to the random variables 𝐩e−pc​(q)σe\frac{\mathbf{p}_{e}-p_{c}(q)}{\sigma_{e}} with γ=1\gamma=1 (using the third condition in the definition of (⋆)NA(\star)^{\text{A}}_{N} and the Brownian scaling), there exists a stopping time T(e)T^{(e)} such that

ℙ[T(e)>t]≲exp[−c′(tσe2)1/3],\mathbb{P}[T^{(e)}>t]\lesssim\exp\left[-c^{\prime}\left(\frac{t}{\sigma_{e}^{2}}\right)^{1/3}\right],

4 Random variables naturally centred near pc​(q)p_{c}(q)

In the previous section we perturbed the environment from the critical one, using variables which were naively centred around the critical point, requiring that the expected value of the random bond parameter was pc​(q)p_{c}(q). The toy example for the analysis was the use of some Brownian motions up to some small time t≪1t\ll 1, whose typical order of magnitude is t\sqrt{t}. Looking more carefully, this approach might look too naive, as one wants a near-critical random environment which remains in the critical phase, therefore neither favouring too much much the primal or the dual model. As our random bond parametrisation is not naturally centred around pcp_{c} from the perspective of self-duality, it is tempting to add a drift correction to the Brownian motions in order to preserve self-duality of the expected random environment up to its second moment. Note that in the natural isoradial parametrisation of the FK model (see e.g. [24]), this drift would vanish. To each of the Brownian motions, we add a drift −μ(q)⋅t-\mu(q)\cdot t, as a natural second order expansion for a random process near 00. In the present section, the critical window in random environment will be expressed via the quantity W~(N)=W(N)(∑r≤NrΔpc(r)4)−1/2\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)=\textrm{W}(N)(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4})^{-1/2}. As CLE computations assert that the mixing rate ι\iota is larger than 12\frac{1}{2} (with equality only at q=4q=4), the multiplicative correction to W​(N)\textrm{W}(N) is conjectured to be of constant order for 1<q<41<q<4 and sub-polynomial for q=4q=4, and so the results should be interpreted as involving the normal critical window W​(N)\textrm{W}(N) instead of W~​(N)\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N).

4.1 The special case of Gaussian variables

4.1.1 Statement of the result and setup of the proof

In this section, we prove an analog of Theorem 1.6 in the special case of a sequence of i.i.d. Gaussian variables whose law is given by

𝐩e​=(d)​𝒩​(pc​(q)−μ⁡(q)​σN,σN2),\mathbf{p}_{e}\overset{(d)}{=}\mathcal{N}(p_{c}(q)-\mu(q)\sigma_{N},\sigma_{N}^{2}), (4.1)

where the parameter σN\sigma_{N} goes to 00 as the size of 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} goes to infinity, which ensures once again that with high probability (i.e. not worsening all the other estimates involved), all the edge weights 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈EN\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} remain in (0,1)(0,1). We use once again i.i.d. Gaussian variables aiming to generalise afterwards by applying Skorohod’s embedding theorem. We modify the i.i.d. Brownian motions from the previous section by adding a linear drift at each edge. Compared to the proof of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4, adding some well chosen drift allows us to lower (with high probability) the order of magnitude of the finite variation processes of the form AtℛA^{\mathcal{R}}_{t} and Ate,fA^{e,f}_{t}, which were identified as being the dominant terms in the respective Itô derivatives. As it will be discussed in Section 4.3, the conceptual reason to subtract that exact drift t↦μ⁡(q)​tt\mapsto\mu(q)t is to construct a random environment under 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} which is on average almost self-dual for its first two moments as in scenario (⋆)NB(\star)_{N}^{\text{B}}. We keep the notations of Section 4.1 and skip most details in the proofs that exactly match those of the previous section. This time, we prove a simplified version of Theorem 1.6 when 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} is given (4.1). Note that Lemma 2.12 ensures that the following result represents a strict improvement of the results obtained in Section 3, as there exists c>0c>0, depending on qq, such that W~​(N)1/3≳W​(N)1/2​Nc\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\gtrsim\textrm{W}(N)^{1/2}N^{c}.

Proposition 4.1.

Fix 1<q≤41<q\leq 4. Assume that the random environment (𝐩e)e∈EN(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} under 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} is given by i.i.d Gaussian satisfying (4.1) for some uniform parameter σN\sigma_{N}. Then there exists some δ=δ⁡(q)>0\delta=\delta(q)>0 and some constant c=c⁡(δ,q)>0c=c(\delta,q)>0 such that for any N≥1N\geq 1 and σN≤c⋅W~​(N)1/3​log⁡(N)−12\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}\log(N)^{-\frac{1}{2}}

𝐏N[ϕ𝕋N,𝔭∈RSW(δ,N)]>1−O(exp[−c⋅(W~​(N)1/3σN)2]).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Bigg]>1-O\left(\exp\Bigg[-c\cdot\Bigg(\frac{\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{1/3}}{\sigma_{N}}\Bigg)^{2}\Bigg]\right).

In this section, for t≥0t\geq 0, one can define the stochastic process 𝔭⁡(t):=(𝐩e​(t))e∈EN\mathfrak{p}(t):=(\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))_{e\in E_{N}}, formed of independent components given by

𝐩e​(t):=pc​(q)+Bt(e)−μ⁡(q)​t,\mathbf{p}_{e}(t):=p_{c}(q)+B^{(e)}_{t}-\mu(q)t,

where t↦Bt(e)t\mapsto B^{(e)}_{t} is a standard Brownian motion attached to the edge ee and we recall the expression μ⁡(q)=q−12​q\mu(q)=\frac{q-1}{2\sqrt{q}}. We are in position to prove Proposition 4.1 in the spirit of the proofs made in Section 3.1, sorting out natural counterparts to Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4. 4.3 Optimality of the random bond near-critical window

In the previous section, we showed that strengthening the condition (⋆)NA(\star)^{\text{A}}_{N} to (⋆)NB(\star)^{\text{B}}_{N} allows us to use a random a random environment where the bonds have a much larger standard deviation. We now explain that a critical window in a random environment of order W​(N)1/3\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3} is “essentially optimal”, in the sense that finding a condition on the (independent) random bond environment 𝔭\mathfrak{p} to enlarge the critical window would require some much more refined understanding than simply the up to constant behaviour of crossing estimates, mixing rates and arm exponents.

Let us start by discussion how the O⁡(σe3)O(\sigma_{e}^{3}) correction term in condition (⋆)NB(\star)^{\text{B}}_{N} naturally appears. In the special case q=1q=1, the results of Section 5 show that the natural condition on the independent random bond parameters is that 𝔼⁡[𝐩e]=12\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}]=\frac{1}{2}, which allows us to preserve the critical phase of the model (at large scale) even with random variables whose standard variation does not decay to 00 as N→∞N\to\infty. When remaining in the near-critical random setup, one may expect that this “criticality condition” generalises to q>1q>1, in the sense that there should exist f=fqf=f_{q} some smooth function depending on qq such that the natural condition on the parameters 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} to preserve criticality at large scales is given by 𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐩e)]=0\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{p}_{e})]=0. While f1f_{1} is easy to guess as it corresponds to asking that the annealed model is critical Bernoulli percolation, this requires some more evolved reasoning when q>1q>1. For q>1q>1, the critical point pc​(q)p_{c}(q) is determined by the fact that it is the self-dual point of the model. In this spirit, the condition we require on fqf_{q} is that 𝔼​[fq​(𝐩)]=0\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\mathbf{p})]=0 for any random variable 𝐩\mathbf{p} which is self-dual for the FK percolation model. By self-dual, we mean that 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝐩∗\mathbf{p}^{*} have the same law, where

𝐩∗:=q⁡(1−𝐩)𝐩+q⁡(1−𝐩)\mathbf{p}^{*}:=\frac{q(1-\mathbf{p})}{\mathbf{p}+q(1-\mathbf{p})}

is the dual parameter of 𝐩\mathbf{p}. Taking 𝐩:=12​δp+12​δp∗\mathbf{p}:=\frac{1}{2}\delta_{p}+\frac{1}{2}\delta_{p^{*}} for p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], this implies that fqf_{q} must satisfy

∀p∈[0,1],fq​(p∗)=−fq​(p).\forall p\in[0,1],\quad f_{q}(p^{*})=-f_{q}(p). (4.5)

In the near-critical setup ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, one can expand near the critical point pc=pc​(q)p_{c}=p_{c}(q) the relation fq​((pc+ε)∗)=−fq​(pc+ε)f_{q}((p_{c}+\varepsilon)^{*})=-f_{q}(p_{c}+\varepsilon), which implies that

which reads as

2​fq​(pc)+0⋅ε+(fq′′​(pc)−q−1q​fq′​(pc))​ε2+(q−1q​fq′′​(pc)−(q−1)2q​fq′​(pc))​ε3+…=02f_{q}(p_{c})+0\cdot\varepsilon+\left(f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c})-\frac{q-1}{\sqrt{q}}f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c})\right)\varepsilon^{2}+\left(\frac{q-1}{\sqrt{q}}f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c})-\frac{(q-1)^{2}}{q}f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c})\right)\varepsilon^{3}+\ldots=0 (4.6)

The above equation shows that if one wants to cancel all the coefficients in the expansion, although there are infinitely many conditions on the derivatives of fqf_{q} at pcp_{c}, these conditions are not sufficient to uniquely determine fqf_{q}. For every n≥1n\geq 1, the condition (4.6) imposes an equation linking the first 2​n2n derivatives at pcp_{c}, but with infinitely many degrees of freedom for fqf_{q}. Indeed, one can freely choose the odd degree derivatives of fqf_{q} at pcp_{c}, which is enough to fix the derivatives of even degree. This can be seen by interpreting (4.5) as asking, up to conjugation by some smooth map, that fqf_{q} is an odd function, whose odd derivatives at zero (corresponding to pcp_{c} under the conjugation) can be chosen arbitrarily, and even derivatives at zero are forced to cancel.

Let us now specify those conditions for the first derivatives of fqf_{q}. This clearly imposes that fq​(pc)=0f_{q}(p_{c})=0. One can always replace fqf_{q} by a constant multiple and still satisfy (4.5), which allws us to arbitrarily fix the value of fq′​(pc)f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c}). Then, (4.6) imposes that fq′′​(pc)=q−1q​fq′​(pc)f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c})=\frac{q-1}{\sqrt{q}}f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c}). Assuming that fqf_{q} is at least three times differentiable at pcp_{c}, plugging in some variable 𝐩\mathbf{p} well concentrated around pcp_{c} in the equation 𝔼​[fq​(𝐩)]=0\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\mathbf{p})]=0, one gets

The link between fq′​(pc)f_{q}^{\prime}(p_{c}) and fq′′​(pc)f_{q}^{\prime\prime}(p_{c}) precisely gives item OPEN2​B)2\textrm{B}) in Definition 1.3.

Now although we do not claim that there does not exist some function fqf_{q} allowing us to have environments which stay critical in a window of size larger than W​(N)1/3\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}, we explain why a generic choice of a function fqf_{q} satisfying (4.5) cannot allow us to go further than W​(N)1/3\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}. Pick a generic fqf_{q} satisfying (4.5) and an environment 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈eN\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in e_{N}} of i.i.d.​ bond parameters such that 𝔼⁡[fq​(𝐩e)]=0\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\mathbf{p}_{e})]=0, and assume by contradiction that the environment can be chosen such that σe≫W​(N)1/3\sigma_{e}\gg\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3}. Now consider the deterministic modification of the environment 𝐩~e=𝐩e+σe3\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}=\mathbf{p}_{e}+\sigma_{e}^{3}. Since 𝔼⁡[fq​(𝐩e)]=0\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\mathbf{p}_{e})]=0, one clearly has 𝔼⁡[fq​(𝐩~e)]=O⁡(σe3)\mathbb{E}[f_{q}(\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e})]=O(\sigma_{e}^{3}). It is not hard to see that it is possible to construct a function f~q\widetilde{f}_{q}, satisfying (4.5) as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 in the following way: under the conjugation map where (4.5) becomes the condition that fqf_{q} is odd, one may pick f~q​(x)=fq​(x)−α​x3\widetilde{f}_{q}(x)=f_{q}(x)-\alpha x^{3} for some well chosen α\alpha. In this construction, f~q\widetilde{f}_{q} obviously depends on the law of the 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} (and so on NN as well), but one may check that α\alpha is bounded uniformly in σe\sigma_{e}, so that even as N→∞N\to\infty and σe→0\sigma_{e}\to 0, one may still consider f~q\widetilde{f}_{q} to be a generic function satisfying (4.5). Now since f~q\widetilde{f}_{q} is a generic function satisfying (4.5), under our assumption, the environment 𝔭~=(𝐩~e)e∈EN\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}=(\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} should still have some RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) property on the torus 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}. However, between the environments 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} and 𝐩~e\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}, the coupling constant differ deterministically by a positive constant σe3≫W​(N)\sigma_{e}^{3}\gg\textrm{W}(N). In particular, assuming 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} remains in the critical phase (with high 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}-probability), this deterministic modification, way above the critical window, imposes that the model with environment 𝔭~\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}} should be super-critical (with high 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}-probability), by simply repeating all the arguments in the proof Theorem 2.3 starting from 𝔭\mathfrak{p} instead of pcp_{c}, and keeping track of the reverse inequalities (see also [25, Section 5]). This is a contradiction, and so a generic choice of fqf_{q} could not lead to critical windows larger than W​(N)1/3\textrm{W}(N)^{1/3} for the random environment.

4.4 Non-independent bonds and extension of the critical window

In this section, we explore the less restrictive setup of bond parameters at each edge that may not be independent. On 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}, we work in a setup where the bonds can be seen as the sum of an i.i.d process at each edge and some (much smaller) correction drift involving the entire random environment in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}. Consider stochastic processes of the form ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)​[𝒮]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}], similar to the one treated in Sections 3.1 and 4.1. One of the key observation when computing d​ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)​[𝒮]\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathcal{S}] is that, with high 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} probability, its dominant term is its finite variation part. Our specific choice of the drift is made here to cancel exactly that drift, making of the processes of the form ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)​[𝒞​(S)]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathscr{C}(S)] pure local martingale, whose stochastic derivatives (estimated via their brackets) are expected to be much smaller, allowing to run some controlled at each scale deformation for a much longer amount of time. In this section, recall the quantity Ξ⁡(N)=(∑r≤Nr​Δpc​(r)2)−1\Xi(N)=(\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{2})^{-1}. Let us note that the inequality Ξ⁡(N)≳W~​(N)2/3\Xi(N)\gtrsim\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{2/3} is essentially sharp (up to subpolynomial factors) when Δpc(R)≳R−1/2+o(1)\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\gtrsim R^{-1/2+o(1)}, but assuming that Δpc(R)≲R−1/2−c\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\lesssim R^{-1/2-c} for some c>0c>0 (which should be the case for q<4q<4), the inequality should hold with an additional polynomial correction Ξ⁡(N)≳Nc′⋅W~​(N)2/3\Xi(N)\gtrsim N^{c^{\prime}}\cdot\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N)^{2/3}, and so the window reached in the following proposition is much larger than that of the previous section. Let us comment on the implications of this statement. Informally speaking, Theorem 1.7 states that, one can correct at each edge the i.i.d Gaussian, whose typical order of magnitude is σN\sigma_{N}, by some random factor, depending on entire environment 𝔭\mathfrak{p}, whose typical order of magnitude is Ξ(N)−1/2⋅σN3≪σN\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\cdot\sigma_{N}^{3}\ll\sigma_{N}, while enlarging the critical window in random environment. ≲|Bt(e)|+t+|ε(e)​(t)|+|ϕ𝔭~​(t)​[ωe]−12|\displaystyle\lesssim|B^{(e)}_{t}|+t+|\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)|+\left|\phi_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]-\frac{1}{2}\right|

One can bound the linear term t≤σN2t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}, while, with probability at least exp⁡(−c​α2)\exp(-c\alpha^{2}), one can bound supt≤σN2|Bt(e)|≤α⋅σN\sup_{t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}}|B_{t}^{(e)}|\leq\alpha\cdot\sigma_{N} for all edges e∈ENe\in E_{N}. Repeating Step 11 of the present proof ensures that with probability at least 1−exp⁡(−c​α2)1-\exp(-c\alpha^{2}), we can bound supt≤σN2|ϕ𝔭~​(t)​[ωe]−12|\sup_{t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}}\left|\phi_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]-\frac{1}{2}\right| by α⋅Ξ(N)−1/2σN\alpha\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\sigma_{N}. Therefore, with probability at least 1−exp⁡(−c​α2)1-\exp(-c\alpha^{2}), one has for any 0≤t≤σN20\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2},

|dd​tε(e)(t)|≲|ε(e)(t)|+α⋅Ξ(N)−1/2σN.\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)\right|\lesssim|\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)|+\alpha\cdot\Xi(N)^{-1/2}\sigma_{N}.

Using Gronwall’s lemma up to time t=σN2≪1t=\sigma_{N}^{2}\ll 1 ensures that, with probability at least 1−exp⁡(−c​α2)1-\exp(-c\alpha^{2}), for any 0≤t≤σN20\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2},

|𝐩~e−𝐩e|=|ε(e)​(t)|≲σN3Ξ​(N)1/2.|\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}-\mathbf{p}_{e}|=|\varepsilon^{(e)}(t)|\lesssim\frac{\sigma_{N}^{3}}{\Xi(N)^{1/2}}.

Proof of Theorem 1.7.

As in the proof of Theorem 1.6, we embed the 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} into Brownian motions with drift 𝐩e​(t)\mathbf{p}_{e}(t), using the stopping times T(e)T^{(e)}. We then define the 𝐩~e​(t)\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t) by setting

𝐩~e​(t)=𝐩e​(t)+ε(e)​(t∧T(e))\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t)=\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)+\varepsilon^{(e)}(t\wedge T^{(e)})

where the ε(e)\varepsilon^{(e)} are determined by ε(e)​(0)=0\varepsilon^{(e)}(0)=0 and the stochastic differential equation (4.7). We can then run the proof as in that of Theorem 1.6, using the crude estimate

𝐏N[supeT(e)>Σ𝔭1/2Ξ(N)3/4]\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{N}\Big[\sup_{e}T^{(e)}>\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{3/4}\Big] ≲N2(exp(−c′(Σ𝔭1/2​Ξ​(N)3/4Σ𝔭2)1/3)+exp(−c′Σ𝔭−1/2))\displaystyle\lesssim N^{2}\left(\exp\left(-c^{\prime}\left(\frac{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\Xi(N)^{3/4}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{2}}\right)^{1/3}\right)+\exp\Big(-c^{\prime}\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-1/2}\Big)\right)
≲exp⁡(−12​c′​(Ξ​(N)1/2Σ𝔭)1/2),\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}c^{\prime}\left(\frac{\Xi(N)^{1/2}}{\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}}\right)^{1/2}\right),
