and conclude the proof from there. ∎

Remark 4.7.

Recall that assuming Δpc(R)≲R−1/2−c\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\lesssim R^{-1/2-c} allows a polynomial improvement in the corrected environment compared to the independent one. We would like to argue here that in this case, the modified variables (𝐩~e)e∈EN(\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} are actually decorrelated in space, in the sense that if ee and ff are two edges far apart in 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N}, the variables 𝐩~e\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e} and 𝐩~f\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{f} are essentially independent. We do not state or prove any result rigorous here. The variable 𝐩~e\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e} can be written as 𝐩e+εT(e)(e)\mathbf{p}_{e}+\varepsilon^{(e)}_{T^{(e)}}, and we now focus on the impact of the correction term εT(e)(e)\varepsilon^{(e)}_{T^{(e)}}, coming from the SDE (4.7). In that equation, the correlations between different 𝐩~e\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e} variables come from the term ϕ𝕋N,𝔭~​(t)​[ωe]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]. But this term is simply a local martingale, given explicitely by Itô’s formula

d​ϕ𝕋N,𝔭~​(t)​[ωe]=∑g∈EN1𝐩~g​(1−𝐩~g)​Cov𝔭~​(t)​(ωe,ωg)​d​Bt(g).\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}]=\sum_{g\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{g}(1-\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{g})}\mathrm{Cov}_{\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}(\omega_{e},\omega_{g})\mathrm{d}B^{(g)}_{t}.

Now assuming that some RSW property and all stability of mixing rates and events hold, the coefficient in front of d​Bt(g)\mathrm{d}B^{(g)}_{t} is of order Δpc​(d⁡(e,g))2\Delta_{p_{c}}(d(e,g))^{2}. Then the derivative of the bracket of this local martingale is of order ∑r≤Nr​Δpc​(r)4≍1\sum_{r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\asymp 1 (this last estimate assumes that Δpc(R)≲R−1/2−c\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)\lesssim R^{-1/2-c}). Furthermore, the contribution from edges gg at distance at least some constant RR from ee to this sum is of order ∑R≤r≤Nr​Δpc​(r)4≍R2​Δpc​(R)4\sum_{R\leq r\leq N}r\Delta_{p_{c}}(r)^{4}\asymp R^{2}\Delta_{p_{c}}(R)^{4}, which goes to 00 as R→∞R\to\infty. Therefore, the local martingale ϕ𝕋N,𝔭~​(t)​[ωe]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}] will mainly depend on edges close to ee, and in the same way the local martingale d​ϕ𝕋N,𝔭~​(t)​[ωf]\mathrm{d}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{f}] will mainly depend on edges close to ff. Hence, if ee and ff are far apart, the process ϕ𝕋N,𝔭~​(t)​[ωe]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{e}] is essentially independent of 𝐩f​(t)\mathbf{p}_{f}(t) and of ϕ𝕋N,𝔭~​(t)​[ωf]\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\widetilde{\mathfrak{p}}(t)}[\omega_{f}]. Plugging this back into (4.7), one gets that the processes 𝐩~e​(t)\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{e}(t) and 𝐩~f​(t)\widetilde{\mathbf{p}}_{f}(t) are essentially independent.

5 The special case of percolation

5.1 Near-critical random bond percolation on the square lattice

Throughout this section, we will be working with q=1q=1. We will prove Theorem 1.8 for bond percolation, first in the special case of i.i.d. Gaussian variables whose law is given by

𝐩e​=(d)​𝒩​(12,σN2),\mathbf{p}_{e}\overset{(d)}{=}\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{1}{2},\sigma_{N}^{2}\right), (5.1)

and then in the general case using once again the Skorokhod embedding theorem. The reason for treating independent bond percolation separately (i.e. separating the proofs for FK percolation of parameter q=1q=1 and the proofs for 1<q≤41<q\leq 4 treated in Sections 3 and 4) is that the near-critical window can be extended up to O⁡(log⁡(N)−2)O(\log(N)^{-2}), almost reaching macroscopic deformations. The previous section showed that for 1<q≤41<q\leq 4, one can pass from a critical window W​(N,q)\textrm{W}(N,q), which is expected to decay like N−ν+o⁡(1)N^{-\nu+o(1)} to near-critical random environments in the larger window W~​(N,q)13=N−ν3+o⁡(1)\widetilde{\textrm{W}}(N,q)^{\frac{1}{3}}=N^{-\frac{\nu}{3}+o(1)} with high 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N}-probability. For Bernoulli percolation, the CLE(6) conjecture implies that for q=1q=1, the critical window is W​(N,q=1)=N−34+o⁡(1)\textrm{W}(N,q=1)=N^{-\frac{3}{4}+o(1)} (which has been rigorously proven for the triangular lattice in [53, 13]). The fact that the near-critical window in a random environment is much larger comes as no surprise, as independence shows that annealed random bond percolation on a random environment where each bond variable is centred at pc​(1)=12p_{c}(1)=\frac{1}{2} has exactly the law of the critical percolation of parameter pc​(1)=12p_{c}(1)=\frac{1}{2}. Moreover, using some hands-on noise sensitivity argument, we prove in Section 5.2 that one can use even larger random variables centred at 12\frac{1}{2} and whose variance is is not bounded from above as N→∞N\to\infty, while keeping the large scale strong box-crossing property with high probability. Unlike the approach used up to here, this result doesn’t assert that crossing probabilities are preserved at every scale, but rather that they are preserved in the large scale regime.

In view of the next proposition, we remark that in the case of Gaussian variables 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e}, the scaling O(log(N)−1/2)O(\log(N)^{-1/2}) corresponds exactly to what is required to ensure that none of the N2N^{2} variables 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} leave the interval [0,1][0,1]. It is remarkable that, up to a constant factor, keeping the 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} from deviating too much from the critical value allows us to keep the RSW property at every scale, as detailed in Proposition 5.1 presented below. As we did previously, we first prove Theorem 1.8 in a simplified Gaussian case and then pass to the general case using Skorokhod embedding theorem. This reads in the following proposition.

Proposition 5.1.

Assume that q=1q=1, and that the random environment (𝐩e)e∈EN(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E_{N}} under 𝐏N\mathbf{P}_{N} is given by i.i.d Gaussian variables satisfying (5.1) with some uniform parameter σN\sigma_{N}. Then there exists some δ>0\delta>0 and some c>0c>0 such that for any N≥1N\geq 1, if σN≤c⋅log(N)−1/2\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\log(N)^{-1/2}, then

𝐏N[ϕ𝕋N,𝔭∈RSW(δ,N)]>1−O(exp(−c⋅σN−2)).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}}\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\Bigg]>1-O\left(\exp\Big(-c\cdot\sigma_{N}^{-2}\Big)\right).

We keep the notations of the previous sections and implement a similar strategy. The main reason behind the improvement from a polynomial to a logarithmic bound lies in the fact that the finite variation processes involved in Proposition 3.1 vanish for percolation due to the independence between edges. Therefore, as it represented the dominant term in the stochastic derivatives of crossings and edge influences, one should only control here the local martingale term. Set once again for t≥0t\geq 0 the process 𝔭⁡(t):=(𝐩e​(t))e∈EN\mathfrak{p}(t):=(\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))_{e\in E_{N}} formed of i.i.d Brownian motions

𝐩e​(t):=pc​(q)+Bt(e),\mathbf{p}_{e}(t):=p_{c}(q)+B^{(e)}_{t},

and still denote by ℱtN\mathcal{F}^{N}_{t} the naturally associated filtration. We intend to prove once again that if t≲log⁡(N)t\lesssim\log(N), all the measures s↦(ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(s))s≤ts\mapsto(\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)})_{s\leq t} remain within the RSW​(δ,N)\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N) class with high probability. In the case of percolation, the independence of edges implies that the mixing rates Δ(e)​(r)\Delta^{(e)}(r) all vanish, making this notion irrelevant. One should therefore go back to the original study of Kesten [38] who studied the scaling relation for percolation via some refined understanding of the 44 arm exponent π4​(r)\pi_{4}(r) at each edge, which encodes the pivotality of edges. We refer to Section 2.3 where this can be explicitely seen in the estimates. Since there are no mixing rates for percolation, the breaking time Tb=Tb​(δ)T_{b}=T_{b}(\delta) is given simply by

Tb:=inf{t≥0|ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)∉RSW​(δ,N)∩(⋂#Stab#​(δ,N))},T_{b}:=\inf\Bigg\{t\geq 0\Bigg|\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}\not\in\textrm{RSW}(\delta,N)\cap\left(\bigcap_{\#}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(\delta,N)\right)\Bigg\},

where once again the intersection is taken on #∈{4,3+,3−,3rg,3lf}\#\in\{4,3^{+},3^{-},3^{\textrm{rg}},3^{\textrm{lf}}\}. As long as 0≤t≤Tb0\leq t\leq T_{b}, the probability 𝐩e​(t)\mathbf{p}_{e}(t) that a the ee is open under the measure ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)} remains bounded away from 00 and 11. One can once again reformulate Proposition 5.1 as the existence of some δ>0\delta>0 and some c>0c>0 such that for σN≤c⋅log(N)−1/2\sigma_{N}\leq c\cdot\log(N)^{-1/2},

𝐏[Tb<σN2]≲exp(−cσN−2).\mathbf{P}\Big[T_{b}<\sigma_{N}^{2}\Big]\lesssim\exp\Big(-c\sigma_{N}^{-2}\Big). (5.2)

Once again, Proposition 5.1 will follow from the following lemma, which is a an adaptation of Lemma 3.3.

Lemma 5.2.

Assume that δ\delta is chosen small enough. There exist some positive constant c=c⁡(δ)>0c=c(\delta)>0 and OδO_{\delta} such that if σN2≤c⋅log⁡(N)−1\sigma_{N}^{2}\leq c\cdot\log(N)^{-1}, one has

𝐏N[∀ 0≤s≤σN2∧Tb,ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(s)∈RSW(2δ,N)]≥1−Oδ(exp(−c⋅1σN2)),\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\ 0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\ \phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\textrm{RSW}(2\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta}\Bigg(\exp\left(-c\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\right)\Bigg),
𝐏N[∀ 0≤s≤σN2∧Tb,ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(s)∈⋂#Stab#(2δ,N)]≥1−Oδ(exp(−c⋅1σN2)).\mathbf{P}_{N}\Bigg[\forall\ 0\leq s\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\ \phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(s)}\in\bigcap_{\#}\textrm{Stab}_{\#}(2\delta,N)\Bigg]\geq 1-O_{\delta}\Bigg(\exp\left(-c\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma_{N}^{2}}\right)\Bigg).
Proof.

We will focus here in the proof of the first estimate, as one can adapt the proof to the second estimate as discussed at the end of the proof of Lemma 4.3. Note that we do not need the events 𝒞∙0​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}^{0}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}) and 𝒞∙⋆1​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}^{\star 1}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}) in this section as boundary conditions have no effect in percolation, so that the RSW property is given simply by estimates on the crossing events 𝒞∙​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}) and 𝒞∙⋆​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}^{\star}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})

Step 0: Canonical decomposition of the semimartingale.

Fix a 22 by 11 rectangle ℛ∈𝕋N\mathcal{R}\in\mathbb{T}_{N}. Using the decomposition of semimartingales, one can write ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)]=Mtℛ+Atℛ\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})]=M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}+A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t} where MℛM^{\mathcal{R}} is a local martingale started at 00 and AℛA^{\mathcal{R}} is an adapted finite variation process, whose exact expression are given by

d​Mtℛ\displaystyle\mathrm{d}M^{\mathcal{R}}_{t} =∑e∈EN1𝐩e​(t)​(1−𝐩e​(t))​Cov𝔭⁡(t)​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)​d​Bt(e)\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}B^{(e)}_{t}
d​Atℛ\displaystyle\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t} =∑e∈EN1𝐩e​(t)​(1−𝐩e​(t))2​(1−1𝐩e​(t)​ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)​[ωe])​Cov𝔭⁡(t)​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)​d​t\displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))^{2}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)}\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]\right)\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})\mathrm{d}t
Step 1: Evaluating the order of magnitude of AtℛA^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}.

In the case of percolation, the edges parameter are independent therefore for any e∈ENe\in E_{N} one has

ϕ𝕋N,𝔭⁡(t)​[ωe]=𝐩e​(t),\phi_{\mathbb{T}_{N},\mathfrak{p}(t)}[\omega_{e}]=\mathbf{p}_{e}(t),

and so d​Atℛ=0\mathrm{d}A^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}=0.

Step 2: Evaluating the order of magnitude of MtℛM^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}.

We estimate once again the rate of growth of the local-martingale MtℛM^{\mathcal{R}}_{t} via some control of its bracket, which is given by

d​⟨Mℛ⟩t=∑e∈EN(1𝐩e​(t)​(1−𝐩e​(t))​Cov𝔭⁡(t)​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)2)​d​t.\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}=\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\left(\frac{1}{\mathbf{p}_{e}(t)(1-\mathbf{p}_{e}(t))}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}\right)\mathrm{d}t.

Using again (3.3), one deduces that

d​⟨Mℛ⟩td​t≍∑e∈ENCov𝔭⁡(t)​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)2.\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\asymp\sum_{e\in E_{N}}\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathfrak{p}(t)}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}. (5.3)

Now Lemma 2.14 allows us to use the critical estimates of Lemma 2.11 to get

∀ 0≤t≤σN2∧Tb,d​⟨Mℛ⟩td​t≲1.\forall\ 0\leq t\leq\sigma_{N}^{2}\wedge T_{b},\quad\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle M^{\mathcal{R}}\rangle_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}\lesssim 1. (5.4)
Step 3: Concluding via large deviations estimates for MtℛM^{\mathcal{R}}_{t}.

We conclude the proof by some straightforward large deviation estimates for the MℛM^{\mathcal{R}} as in the previous section, we omit the details. Once again, adapting for arm events poses no difficulties. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.8.

Once Proposition 5.1 is proven, one can apply once again the Skorokhod embedding theorem as in Section 3 to pass from Brownian motions to a sequence of general random variables satisfying (⋆)Nq=1(\star)^{q=1}_{N}. We simply point out the intermediate estimate which is used

𝐏N[supeT(e)>Σ𝔭1/2]≲exp(−c⋅Σ𝔭−1/2).\mathbf{P}_{N}\left[\sup_{e}T^{(e)}>\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{1/2}\right]\lesssim\exp(-c\cdot\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-1/2}).

∎

5.2 Random bond percolation via noise sensitivity

The goal of this section is to extend, in the large scale limit the RSW box crossing property to deformations from the critical point which are macroscopic, meaning that one doesn’t need to scale the maximal variance Σ𝔭\Sigma_{\mathfrak{p}} inside 𝕋N\mathbb{T}_{N} to 00 as N→∞N\to\infty, working in true random bond context. From the previous section, this theorem comes as no surprise. Indeed, we showed that, in the case of Brownian deformations centred at the critical point, as long as the model stays critical at every scale, the stochastic derivative (5.4) is bounded independently from NN. The only reason that one needs additional logarithmic factors is to brutally ensure that none of the probabilities ϕ𝔭​[𝒞∙​(ℛ)]\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R})] have deviated far from their original value, while one can expect that even if few boxes became too off-critical, it will not have a big influence on the criticality of the large scale model. Therefore, one should find some kind of renormalisation argument to bypass the relevance of criticality being preserved at each scale. The idea to use noise sensitivity in our context is not so surprising. In fact, the key estimate in our proof for showing that RSW holds up to windows of logarithmic size depends essentially on the estimate, for all 22 by 11 rectangles ℛ\mathcal{R},

∑e∈ℤ2Covpc​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)2≲1\sum_{e\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}\lesssim 1

where we point out that the covariance is zero when e∉ℛe\not\in\mathcal{R}. Using half-plane two arm events (see [35, Chapter VI.1]), one can actually also show with the arguments of Section 2.3 that as the width of ℛ\mathcal{R} goes to infinity,

∑e∈ℤ2Covpc​(𝒞∙​(ℛ),ωe)2→0.\sum_{e\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}}\mathrm{Cov}_{p_{c}}(\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}),\omega_{e})^{2}\to 0. (5.5)

This is exactly the usual condition used to show that the event 𝒞∙​(ℛ)\mathscr{C}_{\bullet}(\mathcal{R}) is asymptotically noise sensitive as the side length of ℛ\mathcal{R} goes to infinity, see [10, Theorem 1.3]. The main difficulty with our method is that it requires that the RSW property is preserved at all scales and in all boxes, which is not enough to prove that (5.5) is preserved up to macroscopic deformations. Still, one wants to use this intuition, which hints that the missing renormalisation argument can be derived via some noise sensitivity of Bernoulli percolation, heavily studied in [10, 34, 54]. We end up using a rather hands-on argument to conclude. Let us start with a sequence of random variables 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈E⁡(ℤ2)\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})}, chosen under some probability measure 𝐏\mathbf{P} such that

  1. 1.

    The variables 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} are mutually independent.

  2. 2.

    For each edge ee, one has 𝔼⁡[𝐩e]=12\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}]=\frac{1}{2}

  3. 3.

    There is some ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that almost surely, all of the 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} belong to [ε,1−ε][\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon].

We denote by ϕ𝔭\phi_{\mathfrak{p}} the associated full-plane percolation measure. We are now in position to state the asymptotic strong box crossing property for crossings. Denote by SNS_{N} a square of side-length NN in the plane.

Proposition 5.3.

Assume that the variables 𝔭\mathfrak{p} satisfy the above conditions. Then as N→∞N\to\infty, one has the following convergence in probability

ϕ𝔭​[𝒞h​(SN)]→(ℙ)12.\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N})]\xlongrightarrow{(\mathbb{P})}\frac{1}{2}.

We start by proving a particular case of the result above, which is actually just a rewording of noise sensitivity of crossing events for percolation.

Lemma 5.4 (A simple consequence of [10, 35]).

Assume 𝔭ε=(𝐩eε)e\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}=(\mathbf{p}_{e}^{\varepsilon})_{e} has the specific following law: the 𝐩eε\mathbf{p}_{e}^{\varepsilon} are i.i.d. variables equal to ε\varepsilon or 1−ε1-\varepsilon, each with probability 12\frac{1}{2}. Then the result of proposition 5.3 holds.

Proof.

Consider a realisation 𝔭ε\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon} of the environment. We define a percolation configuration ωe​n​v\mathbf{\omega}_{env} by setting ωe​n​v​(e)\omega_{env}(e) to be open if 𝐩eε=1−ε\mathbf{p}_{e}^{\varepsilon}=1-\varepsilon, and closed otherwise. Note that ωe​n​v​(e)\omega_{env}(e) is a deterministic function of the environment 𝔭ε\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}, but its annealed law is that of critical percolation, because each 𝐩eε\mathbf{p}^{\varepsilon}_{e} is independently ε\varepsilon or 1−ε1-\varepsilon with probability 12\frac{1}{2}.

Now consider the following way of sampling the percolation configuration ω\omega from the random bond percolation ϕ𝔭ε\phi_{\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}}: one starts with ωe​n​v\omega_{env}, and for each edge ee, one flips the state of edge ee with probability ε\varepsilon. Indeed, if for example ωe​n​v​(e)=0\omega_{env}(e)=0, this means that 𝐩e=ε\mathbf{p}_{e}=\varepsilon, and so ω⁡(e)=0=ωe​n​v​(e)\omega(e)=0=\omega_{env}(e) with probability 1−ε1-\varepsilon, and ω⁡(e)=1=1−ωe​n​v​(e)\omega(e)=1=1-\omega_{env}(e) with probability ε\varepsilon, independently at each edge. Then [10, Theorem 1.2] states that the crossing events 𝒞h​(SN)\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N}) are asymptotically noise sensitive as N→∞N\to\infty. According to [35, Exercise IV.6], this is equivalent to saying that 𝐏[ω∈𝒞h(SN)|ωe​n​v]−𝐏[ω∈𝒞h(SN)]\mathbf{P}[\omega\in\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N})|\omega_{env}]-\mathbf{P}[\omega\in\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N})] converges to 00 in probability. But under the annealed probability measure 𝐏\mathbf{P}, ω\omega is simply a Bernoulli percolation with parameter 12\frac{1}{2}, so 𝐏⁡[𝒞h​(SN)]→12\mathbf{P}[\mathscr{C}_{h}(S_{N})]\to\frac{1}{2} as N→∞N\to\infty. This exactly gives the desired result. ∎

We now pass to the proof of Proposition 5.3 for a general set of independent random variables.

Proof.

Let 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈E⁡(ℤ2)\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})} be random variables satisfying the above condition. We will write the environment 𝔭\mathfrak{p} as some averaged version of the environment 𝔭ε\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon}. Given a realisation 𝔭=(𝐩e)e∈E⁡(ℤ2)\mathfrak{p}=(\mathbf{p}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})} of the environment, one can define random variables (𝐪e)e∈E⁡(ℤ2)(\mathbf{q}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})} as follows: for each edge ee, take 𝐪e\mathbf{q}_{e} to be

𝐪e:={ε with probability ​1−ε−𝐩e1−2​ε1−ε with probability ​𝐩e−ε1−2​ε,\mathbf{q}_{e}:=\begin{cases}\varepsilon&\text{ with probability }\frac{1-\varepsilon-\mathbf{p}_{e}}{1-2\varepsilon}\\ 1-\varepsilon&\text{ with probability }\frac{\mathbf{p}_{e}-\varepsilon}{1-2\varepsilon},\end{cases}

in a way that the variables 𝐪e\mathbf{q}_{e} are independent, both unconditionally and conditionally on 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. Note that this definition makes sense precisely because 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} is almost surely in [ε;1−ε][\varepsilon;1-\varepsilon], and it is straightforward to see that 𝔼⁡[𝐪e|𝔭]=𝐩e\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{q}_{e}|\mathfrak{p}]=\mathbf{p}_{e}. Consider the random environment 𝔮=(𝐪e)e∈E⁡(ℤ2)\mathfrak{q}=(\mathbf{q}_{e})_{e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2})}. Not conditioning anymore on the random variables 𝔭\mathfrak{p}, this environment 𝔮\mathfrak{q} has independent bonds taking values in {ε,1−ε}\{\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon\}, and it satisfies, for each e∈E⁡(ℤ2)e\in E(\mathbb{Z}^{2}), 𝔼⁡[𝐪e]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[𝐪e|𝔭]]=𝔼⁡[𝐩e]=12\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{q}_{e}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{q}_{e}|\mathfrak{p}]]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{p}_{e}]=\frac{1}{2}. Therefore, 𝔮\mathfrak{q} actually has the law of the environment 𝔭ε\mathfrak{p}^{\varepsilon} given in Lemma 5.4. This allows to conclude that for any γ>0\gamma>0,

𝐏[|ϕ𝔮[𝒞(SN)]−12|>γ]⟶N→∞0,\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>\gamma\Bigg]\underset{N\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0,

which, by Markov’s inequality, implies that

𝐏[𝐏[|ϕ𝔮[𝒞(SN)]−12|>γ|𝔭]>γ]⟶N→∞0.\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>\gamma\ \Bigg|\mathfrak{p}\Bigg]>\gamma\Bigg]\underset{N\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0.

To conclude, it is enough to notice that to sample the percolation configuration ω\omega under ϕ𝔭\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}, one can first sample 𝔮\mathfrak{q} from 𝔭\mathfrak{p}, and then sample ω\omega from ϕ𝔮\phi_{\mathfrak{q}} (as 𝔼⁡[𝐪e|𝔭]=𝐩e\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{q}_{e}|\mathfrak{p}]=\mathbf{p}_{e}). Therefore

ϕ𝔭​[𝒞⁡(SN)]=𝔼⁡[ϕ𝔮​[𝒞⁡(SN)]|𝔭],\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]|\mathfrak{p}],

which allows to write

|ϕ𝔭​[𝒞⁡(SN)]−12|\displaystyle\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right| ≤𝔼⁡[|ϕ𝔮​[𝒞⁡(SN)]−12||𝔭]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|\ \Bigg|\mathfrak{p}\Bigg]
≤γ+𝐏⁡[|ϕ𝔮​[𝒞⁡(SN)]−12|>γ|𝔭].\displaystyle\leq\gamma+\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>\gamma\ \Bigg|\mathfrak{p}\Bigg].

This allows to conclude that

𝐏[|ϕ𝔭[𝒞(SN)]−12|>2γ]≤𝐏[𝐏[|ϕ𝔮[𝒞(SN)]−12|>γ|𝔭]>γ]⟶N→∞0.\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>2\gamma\Bigg]\leq\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\mathbf{P}\Bigg[\left|\phi_{\mathfrak{q}}[\mathscr{C}(S_{N})]-\frac{1}{2}\right|>\gamma\ \Bigg|\mathfrak{p}\Bigg]>\gamma\Bigg]\underset{N\to\infty}{\longrightarrow}0.

This concludes the proof. ∎

Let us now move on to proving that Cardy’s formula stays true in a random environment.

Proof of Theorem 1.10.

Fix some x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1], and consider the crossing event denoted FN​(x)=𝒞⁡([CN;AN],[xN;BN])F_{N}(x)=\mathcal{C}([C_{N};A_{N}],[x_{N};B_{N}]). If x=0x=0 or x=1x=1, then ϕ𝔭​[FN​(x)]\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)] is identically 00 or 11 respectively. Assuming that x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), we claim that as N→∞N\to\infty, the events FN​(x)F_{N}(x) are asymptotically noise-sensitive. Indeed, one can follow the same computations as in [35, Chapter VI.1] by considering the quadrilateral AN​BN​xN​CNA_{N}B_{N}x_{N}C_{N}. The key point is that all of the sides of this quadrilateral are straight lines, so one can use half-plane three arm events, and the corners have an opening angle of π\pi at xNx_{N} and π/3≤π\pi/3\leq\pi at AN,BN,CNA_{N},B_{N},C_{N} (see Figure 1 in the introduction), so one can use half-plane two arm events to control pivotality in the corners. Then one can run the proof of Proposition 5.3 to get that as N→∞N\to\infty,

ϕ𝔭​[FN​(x)]−𝐏⁡[FN​(x)]→(ℙ)0.\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]-\mathbf{P}[F_{N}(x)]\xlongrightarrow{(\mathbb{P})}0.

Once again, the annealed model is simply critical Bernoulli percolation, which ensures via Theorem 1.9 that one has ℙ​[FN​(x)]→1−x\mathbb{P}[F_{N}(x)]\to 1-x as N→∞N\to\infty. Therefore, one gets that ϕ𝔭​[FN​(x)]\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)] converges to 1−x1-x in probability as N→∞N\to\infty.

Now we quickly explain how to pass from this “pointwise” convergence in probability to the “uniform” convergence in probability of Theorem 1.10. This is a basic consequence of the fact that the x↦ϕ𝔭​[FN​(x)]x\mapsto\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)] are increasing. Indeed, fix some KK and consider xi=iKx_{i}=\frac{i}{K} for i=0,1,…,Ki=0,1,\ldots,K. We may take NN large enough so that for each ii, one has

𝐏[|ϕ𝔭[FN(xi)]−xi|>1/K]≤1K⁡(K+1).\mathbf{P}\big[|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x_{i})]-x_{i}|>1/K\big]\leq\frac{1}{K(K+1)}.

so that by a union bound,

𝐏[∀ 0≤i≤K,|ϕ𝔭[FN(xi)]−xi|≤1/K]>1−1/K.\mathbf{P}\big[\forall\ 0\leq i\leq K,\quad|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x_{i})]-x_{i}|\leq 1/K\big]>1-1/K.

Under this event, for each x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), let ii be the index such that xi≤x<xi+1x_{i}\leq x<x_{i+1}. Then we may write

xi−1/K≤ϕ𝔭​[FN​(xi)]≤ϕ𝔭​[FN​(x)]≤ϕ𝔭​[FN​(xi+1)]≤xi+1+1/K.x_{i}-1/K\leq\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x_{i})]\leq\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]\leq\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x_{i+1})]\leq x_{i+1}+1/K.

Plugging in the fact that xi+1≤x+1/Kx_{i+1}\leq x+1/K and xi≥x−1/Kx_{i}\geq x-1/K gives that |ϕ𝔭​[FN​(x)]−x|≤2/K{|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]-x|\leq 2/K}. Therefore, for NN large enough,

𝐏[∀x∈[0,1],|ϕ𝔭[FN(x)]−x|≤2/K]>1−1/K\mathbf{P}\big[\forall\ x\in[0,1],\quad|\phi_{\mathfrak{p}}[F_{N}(x)]-x|\leq 2/K\big]>1-1/K

Taking N→∞N\to\infty and K→∞K\to\infty sufficiently slowly gives exactly the statement of Theorem 1.10. ∎

A.2 Proofs of crossing estimates via arm events

We collect here the proofs of geometric estimates stated in Section 2.3. In these proofs, we do not detail the geometric estimates based on RSW, and for the sake of readability, we will often identify lengths at the same scale, for example instead of writing “there is a four-arm event from scales 2​r2r to R/2R/2”, we would write “there is a four-arm event from scales rr to RR”.

Proof of Lemma 2.7.

Appendix B Estimates on Skorokhod embedding stopping times

B.1 Tails for Skorokhod embedding stopping times

In this section, we prove Lemma 3.6. We point out that when the random variable XX is bounded, there are simpler arguments that show that TT has exponential tails (which is the case γ=∞\gamma=\infty).

Proof of Lemma 3.6.

The goal will be to use the so-called Vallois embedding [55] in order to construct some stopping time TT adapted to a standard Brownian motion (Bt)t≥0(B_{t})_{t\geq 0} such that BT​=(d)​XB_{T}\overset{(d)}{=}X. We denote ℱt:=σ(Bs,0≤s≤t)\mathcal{F}_{t}:=\sigma\Big(B_{s},0\leq s\leq t\Big) the naturally associated filtration. Let us recall explicitly this construction here, which corresponds to [17] in the special case where h⁡(s)=sh(s)=s and F=0F=0. We mostly keep the notations of [17] in order to simplify cross-reading between the articles. All the constants involved in the statements depend only on cc and γ\gamma. Let μ\mu be the law of the random variable XX and set for x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} its potential denoted Uμ​(x)U_{\mu}(x) (which is related to the function c⁡(x)c(x) in [17]) and given by

Uμ(x):=−∫ℝ|x−y|dμ(y)=−x−2∫x∞(y−x)dμ(y).U_{\mu}(x):=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}|x-y|d\mu(y)=-x-2\int_{x}^{\infty}(y-x)d\mu(y).

This allows to define the functions θ,ϕ,R,S,Γ\theta,\phi,R,S,\Gamma as:

{θ⁡(s):=argminx>0​{−s−Uμ​(x)x},ϕ⁡(s):=argmaxx<0​{−s−Uμ​(x)x},{R⁡(s):=−s−Uμ​(θ​(s))θ⁡(s),S⁡(s):=−s−Uμ​(ϕ​(s))ϕ⁡(s),Γ⁡(s):=R⁡(s)−S⁡(s)2.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\theta(s):=\textrm{argmin}_{x>0}\left\{\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(x)}{x}\right\},\\ \phi(s):=\textrm{argmax}_{x<0}\left\{\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(x)}{x}\right\},\end{array}\right.\quad\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}R(s):=\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(\theta(s))}{\theta(s)},\\ S(s):=\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(\phi(s))}{\phi(s)},\\ \Gamma(s):=\frac{R(s)-S(s)}{2}.\end{array}\right.

One can then parametrize the time using H⁡(s):=∫0sd​zΓ⁡(z)H(s):=\int_{0}^{s}\frac{dz}{\Gamma(z)} and define the reparametrized versions of θ\theta and ϕ\phi by setting:

a⁡(ℓ):=θ⁡(H−1​(ℓ)),b⁡(ℓ):=ϕ⁡(H−1​(ℓ)).a(\ell):=\theta(H^{-1}(\ell)),\quad b(\ell):=\phi(H^{-1}(\ell)).

Let LtL_{t} be the local time of BtB_{t} at 00 [40]. The Vallois stopping time [55] is given by [17, Equation (2)] to the filtration ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} and is defined by

TV:=inf{t≥0|Bt∉(b⁡(Lt),a⁡(Lt))}.T_{V}:=\inf\{t\geq 0|B_{t}\not\in(b(L_{t}),a(L_{t}))\}. (B.1)

The main goal of this section is to obtain tail estimates for the variable TVT_{V}. In order to simplify the reading, we assume that the law μ\mu has a density with respect to the Lebesgue measure (denoted here by ff), but the announced results hold in full generality. Given the formulation θ⁡(s)\theta(s) as an argmax on ℝ+∗\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*}, it is straightforward to see that

dd​x​(−s−Uμ​(x)x)|x=θ⁡(s)\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{-s-U_{\mu}(x)}{x}\right)|_{x=\theta(s)} =dd​x​(−s+2​∫x∞(y−x)​f​(y)​𝑑yx+1)|x=θ⁡(s)\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{-s+2\int_{x}^{\infty}(y-x)f(y)dy}{x}+1\right)|_{x=\theta(s)}
=s−2​∫θ⁡(s)∞y​f​(y)​𝑑yθ​(s)2=0,\displaystyle=\frac{s-2\int_{\theta(s)}^{\infty}yf(y)dy}{\theta(s)^{2}}=0,

which ensures that

s=2∫θ⁡(s)∞yf(y)dy≲exp(−c⋅θ(s)γ).s=2\int_{\theta(s)}^{\infty}yf(y)dy\lesssim\exp(-c\cdot\theta(s)^{\gamma}).

The above equation reads as θ⁡(s)≲log⁡(1/s)1/γ\theta(s)\lesssim\log(1/s)^{1/\gamma}, and the same estimate holds by symmetry for −ϕ⁡(s)-\phi(s). This ensures that as long as ss remains far away from 00 and ∞\infty, both functions θ,−ϕ\theta,-\phi remain also bounded away from 00 and ∞\infty. In order to finish the proof, one needs to estimate all three functions R,S,ΓR,S,\Gamma in the s→0s\to 0 regime. One has

Γ(s)=1−(μ[θ(s),∞)−μ(−∞,ϕ(s)]).\Gamma(s)=1-\big(\mu[\theta(s),\infty)-\mu(-\infty,\phi(s)]\big).

It is clear from the definitions of θ⁡(s)\theta(s) and ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s) that when s→0s\to 0, the functions θ⁡(s),−ϕ⁡(s)\theta(s),-\phi(s) diverge to +∞+\infty, which ensure that Γ\Gamma is bounded from below and H⁡(s)H(s) grows at linear speed when s→0s\to 0. Fix some ε>0\varepsilon>0 (which will be adjusted later in the proof). Using the union bound, for any t>0t>0, one can write

ℙ[T∗>t]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big[T^{*}>t\Big] ≤ℙ⁡[T∗>t,Lt/2>ε]+ℙ⁡[T∗>t,Lt/2≤ε]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\Big[T^{*}>t,L_{t/2}>\varepsilon\Big]+\mathbb{P}\Big[T^{*}>t,L_{t/2}\leq\varepsilon\Big]
≤ℙ[sups≤t/2|Bs|<2log(1/ε)1/γ]+ℙ[Lt/2≤ε]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left[\sup_{s\leq t/2}|B_{s}|<2\log(1/\varepsilon)^{1/\gamma}\right]+\mathbb{P}\Big[L_{t/2}\leq\varepsilon\Big]
≲exp⁡(−clog⁡(1/ε)2/γ​t)+εt.\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\left(\frac{-c}{\log(1/\varepsilon)^{2/\gamma}}t\right)+\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{t}}.

Set ε=exp⁡(−tγγ+2)\varepsilon=\exp\left(-t^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\right), which ensures that for t≳1t\gtrsim 1 one has, for c>0c>0 small enough,

ℙ[TV>t]≲ℙ[T∗>t/2]+exp(−ct)≲exp(−ctγγ+2),\mathbb{P}\Big[T_{V}>t\Big]\lesssim\mathbb{P}\Big[T^{*}>t/2\Big]+\exp(-ct)\lesssim\exp\left(-ct^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\right),

since γγ+2≤1\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}\leq 1, which concludes the proof. ∎

B.2 Tails for Skorokhod embedding stopping times with drift

In this section, we prove Lemma 4.5. Once again, when XX is bounded, one may show that the result holds with γ=∞\gamma=\infty.

Proof of Lemma 4.5.

Set Yt=Bt−μ​tY_{t}=B_{t}-\mu t. From the process (Yt)t≥0(Y_{t})_{t\geq 0}, one can naturally construct a martingale Zt=e2​μ​Yt−1Z_{t}=e^{2\mu Y_{t}}-1 such that Z0=0Z_{0}=0 almost surely. The Dubins-Schwarz Theorem ensures the existence of a Brownian motion B~\widetilde{B} adapted to some modified filtration (potentially defined on some extended probability space), such that Zt=B~⟨Z,Z⟩tZ_{t}=\widetilde{B}_{\langle Z,Z\rangle_{t}}. Applying the Skorokhod embedding theorem recalled above to the centred random variable e2​μ​X−1e^{2\mu X}-1, there exists some stopping time TVT_{V} such that B~TV​=(d)​e2​μ​X−1\widetilde{B}_{T_{V}}\overset{(d)}{=}e^{2\mu X}-1. One can then define the stopping time

T:=inf{t≥0|⟨Z,Z⟩t=TV}.T:=\inf\{t\geq 0|\langle Z,Z\rangle_{t}=T_{V}\}.

Let us see why this TT satisfies the first condition of the lemma. One can couple (Y,B~,TV)(Y,\widetilde{B},T_{V}) to XX in such a way that B~TV=e2​μ​X−1\widetilde{B}_{T_{V}}=e^{2\mu X}-1. Then one may write, on the event that {T<∞}\{T<\infty\},

e2​μ​X−1=B~TV=B~⟨Z,Z⟩T=ZT=e2​μ​YT−1e^{2\mu X}-1=\widetilde{B}_{T_{V}}=\widetilde{B}_{\langle Z,Z\rangle_{T}}=Z_{T}=e^{2\mu Y_{T}}-1

Since x↦e2​μ​X−1x\mapsto e^{2\mu X}-1 is injective, one gets that X=YTX=Y_{T} on the event {T<∞}\{T<\infty\}.

Given the definition of TT, it is not mandatory that ⟨Z,Z⟩t→∞\langle Z,Z\rangle_{t}\to\infty as t→∞t\to\infty, therefore the event {T=∞}\{T=\infty\} may happen with positive probability. Still, in the regime σ≪1\sigma\ll 1 which is relevant in our setup, this will happen with a small probability depending on σ\sigma. Fix some parameter ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1, whose value will be fixed later in the reasoning. In order to estimate the tail of the stopping time TT, one can make the dichotomy

ℙ[T>t]≤ℙ[TV>μt]+ℙ[T>TV/μ,TV≤μt].\mathbb{P}\Big[T>t\Big]\leq\mathbb{P}\Big[T_{V}>\mu t\Big]+\mathbb{P}\Big[T>T_{V}/\mu,T_{V}\leq\mu t\Big]. (B.2)

Combining the fact that |X|≤1|X|\leq 1 and that μ\mu is bounded away from 00 and ∞\infty ensures that e2​μ​X−1e^{2\mu X}-1 also has the same stretched exponential tail as XX. Therefore

ℙ[TV>μt]≲exp(−c′⋅(tσ2)γγ+2)\mathbb{P}\Big[T_{V}>\mu t\Big]\lesssim\exp\Big(-c^{\prime}\cdot\Big(\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\Big)

for some constant c′c^{\prime} only depending on cc. In order to derive tails bounds for the the stopping time TT, it remains to evaluate the second term in the RSH of (B.2). One has

ℙ⁡[T>TV/μ,TV≤μ​t]=ℙ⁡[⟨Z,Z⟩TV/μ<TV,TV≤μ​t]\mathbb{P}\Big[T>T_{V}/\mu,T_{V}\leq\mu t\Big]=\mathbb{P}\Big[\langle Z,Z\rangle_{T_{V}/\mu}<T_{V},T_{V}\leq\mu t\Big]

Computing explicitly the bracket of ZZ, one gets

⟨Z,Z⟩TV/μ=2​μ​∫0TV/μe2​μ​Yt​𝑑t≥2​TV⋅exp⁡(2​μ​(inf0≤s≤TV/μYs)).\langle Z,Z\rangle_{T_{V}/\mu}=2\mu\int_{0}^{T_{V}/\mu}e^{2\mu Y_{t}}\mathrm{d}t\geq 2T_{V}\cdot\exp\Big(2\mu\Big(\inf_{0\leq s\leq T_{V}/\mu}Y_{s}\Big)\Big).

Let μTV\mu_{T_{V}} be the law of the stopping time TVT_{V}. The previous equation implies that

ℙ⁡[⟨Z,Z⟩TV/μ<TV,TV≤μ​t]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big[\langle Z,Z\rangle_{T_{V}/\mu}<T_{V},T_{V}\leq\mu t\Big] ≤ℙ[inf0≤s≤TV/μYs<−log⁡22​μ,TV≤μt]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq T_{V}/\mu}Y_{s}<-\frac{\log 2}{2\mu},T_{V}\leq\mu t\right]
=∫0μ​tℙ[inf0≤s≤u/μYs<−log⁡22​μ]dμTV(u)\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\mu t}\mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq u/\mu}Y_{s}<-\frac{\log 2}{2\mu}\right]d\mu_{T_{V}}(u)
≤∫0μ​tℙ[inf0≤s≤u/μBs<u−log⁡22​μ]dμTV(u).\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{\mu t}\mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq u/\mu}B_{s}<u-\frac{\log 2}{2\mu}\right]d\mu_{T_{V}}(u).

Assuming that tt is chosen smaller than some constant depending on μ\mu, and that μ​t\mu t is not an atom of μTV\mu_{T_{V}}, there exist c1,c2,c3>0c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}>0, only depending on c,γ,μc,\gamma,\mu such that

∫0μ​tℙ[inf0≤s≤u/μBs<u−log⁡22​μ]dμTV(u)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\mu t}\mathbb{P}\left[\inf_{0\leq s\leq u/\mu}B_{s}<u-\frac{\log 2}{2\mu}\right]d\mu_{T_{V}}(u) ≲∫0μ​texp⁡(−c1u)​d​μTV​(u)\displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{\mu t}\exp\Big(-\frac{c_{1}}{u}\Big)d\mu_{T_{V}}(u)
≲(∫0μ​texp⁡(−c2u−c2⋅(uσ2)γγ+2)​𝑑u)\displaystyle\lesssim\Bigg(\int_{0}^{\mu t}\exp\Big(-\frac{c_{2}}{u}-c_{2}\cdot\Big(\frac{u}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\Big)du\Bigg)
+exp⁡(−c2t−c2⋅(tσ2)γγ+2)\displaystyle\qquad+\exp\Big(-\frac{c_{2}}{t}-c_{2}\cdot\Big(\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\Big)
≲exp(−c3⋅σ−γγ+1)+exp(−c3⋅(tσ2)γγ+2),\displaystyle\lesssim\exp\Big(-c_{3}\cdot\sigma^{-\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+1}}\Big)+\exp\Big(-c_{3}\cdot\Big(\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\Big)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\Big),

where the passage from the first to the second line is made by integration by parts and the passage to the last line is simply a weighted arithmetic mean-geometric mean inequality. Combining everything, there exists a constant c4>0c_{4}>0 such that for tt smaller than some constant,

ℙ[T>t]≲exp(−c4⋅σ−γγ+1)+exp(−c4(tσ2)γγ+2).\mathbb{P}\Big[T>t\Big]\lesssim\exp\Big(-c_{4}\cdot\sigma^{-\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+1}}\Big)+\exp\left(-c_{4}\left(\frac{t}{\sigma^{2}}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+2}}\right).

Note that this inequality extends to all tt because of the first term which is constant in tt and dominates as long as t≫σγ/(γ+1)t\gg\sigma^{\gamma/(\gamma+1)}. This first term encapsulates the fact that TT may be very large (or even infinite) because ⟨Z,Z⟩t\langle Z,Z\rangle_{t} does not tend to ∞\infty almost surely, and so this first term is notably a bound for ℙ[T=∞]\mathbb{P}[T=\infty]. Conversely, when t≪σγγ+1t\ll\sigma^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma+1}} (which is much larger than σ\sigma), it is the second term which dominates. ∎

B.3 Large deviation principles for sums of random variables with stretched exponential tails

Finally, in this section, we follow a strategy similar to [4] to prove Lemma 3.7.

Proof of Lemma 3.7.

First start by separating the probability

ℙ[X>t]≤ℙ[supi(aiTi)>t]+ℙ[X>t,supi(aiTi)≤T]\mathbb{P}[X>t]\leq\mathbb{P}\left[\sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})>t\right]+\mathbb{P}\left[X>t,\ \sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})\leq T\right]

The first term of the RHS of the above equation can be estimated by a simple union bound, using the fact that t≳St\gtrsim S:

ℙ[supi(aiTi)>t]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})>t\right] ≲∑iexp⁡(−c​(tai)γ)≲∑iaiS​exp⁡(−c2​(tai)γ)\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{i}\exp\left(-c\left(\frac{t}{a_{i}}\right)^{\gamma}\right)\lesssim\sum_{i}\frac{a_{i}}{S}\exp\left(-\frac{c}{2}\left(\frac{t}{a_{i}}\right)^{\gamma}\right)
≤exp⁡(−c2​(tm)γ).\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(-\frac{c}{2}\left(\frac{t}{m}\right)^{\gamma}\right).

We pass to the second term. Here, we introduce a parameter λ\lambda, which we set equal to λ:=c​tγ−12​mγ\lambda:=\frac{ct^{\gamma-1}}{2m^{\gamma}}. Then we may write

ℙ[X>t,supi(aiTi)≤T]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[X>t,\ \sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})\leq T\right] ≤e−λ​t​∏i𝔼⁡[eλ​ai​Ti​𝟙​(ai​Ti≤t)]\displaystyle\leq e^{-\lambda t}\prod_{i}\mathbb{E}\big[e^{\lambda a_{i}T_{i}}\mathbbm{1}(a_{i}T_{i}\leq t)\big]
≤exp⁡(−λ​t+∑i𝔼⁡[(eλ​ai​Ti−1)​𝟙​(ai​Ti≤t)]).\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(-\lambda t+\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}\big[(e^{\lambda a_{i}T_{i}}-1)\mathbbm{1}(a_{i}T_{i}\leq t)\big]\right).

We now estimate the expectations inside the exponential. Write ℙTi\mathbb{P}_{T_{i}} for the law of TiT_{i}, then using integration by parts, one gets (as long as t/ait/a_{i} is not an atom of TiT_{i}, while there are only countably many tt where this can occur),

𝔼⁡[(eλ​ai​Ti−1)​𝟙​(ai​Ti≤t)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[(e^{\lambda a_{i}T_{i}}-1)\mathbbm{1}(a_{i}T_{i}\leq t)\big] =λ​ai​∫0t/aieλ​ai​s​ℙTi​([s,t/ai])​𝑑s≲λ​ai​∫0t/aieλ​ai​s−c​sγ​𝑑s.\displaystyle=\lambda a_{i}\int_{0}^{t/a_{i}}e^{\lambda a_{i}s}\mathbb{P}_{T_{i}}([s,t/a_{i}])ds\lesssim\lambda a_{i}\int_{0}^{t/a_{i}}e^{\lambda a_{i}s-cs^{\gamma}}ds.

For s≤t/ais\leq t/a_{i}, one may use that 0<γ<10<\gamma<1 to write that

λ​ai​s≤c​tγ−12​mγ​ai​(tai)1−γ​sγ≤c2​sγ.\lambda a_{i}s\leq\frac{ct^{\gamma-1}}{2m^{\gamma}}a_{i}\left(\frac{t}{a_{i}}\right)^{1-\gamma}s^{\gamma}\leq\frac{c}{2}s^{\gamma}.

Hence one may bound the integral ∫0t/aieλ​ai​s−c​sγ​𝑑s\int_{0}^{t/a_{i}}e^{\lambda a_{i}s-cs^{\gamma}}ds by ∫0∞e−csγ/2ds\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-cs^{\gamma}/2}ds which is a finite constant depending only on cc. From this, one gets that 𝔼⁡[(eλ​ai​Ti−1)​𝟙​(ai​Ti≤t)]≲λ​ai\mathbb{E}[(e^{\lambda a_{i}T_{i}}-1)\mathbbm{1}(a_{i}T_{i}\leq t)]\lesssim\lambda a_{i}. Putting everything together and using the value of λ\lambda, we obtain

ℙ[X>t,supi(aiTi)≤T]≤exp(−c2(tm)γ+Ktγ−1mγS),\mathbb{P}\left[X>t,\ \sup_{i}(a_{i}T_{i})\leq T\right]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{c}{2}\left(\frac{t}{m}\right)^{\gamma}+K\frac{t^{\gamma-1}}{m^{\gamma}}S\right),

where KK is a constant depending on cc, which can be made explicit depending on cc and the constant of the ≲\lesssim in the previous equation. Now we set CC to be C:=4​KcC:=\frac{4K}{c} so that if t≥C​St\geq CS, one may write K​tγ−1mγ​S≤c4​(tm)γK\frac{t^{\gamma-1}}{m^{\gamma}}S\leq\frac{c}{4}\left(\frac{t}{m}\right)^{\gamma} and therefore for t≥C​St\geq CS, one gets

ℙ[X>t]≲exp(−c4(tm)γ).\mathbb{P}[X>t]\lesssim\exp\left(-\frac{c}{4}\left(\frac{t}{m}\right)^{\gamma}\right).

This concludes the proof. ∎
